edus.text: If sustained European colonization of the Americas had begun around 1092 instead of 1492, the trajectory of global history would have shifted dramatically.
But not simply by moving the familiar Age of Exploration four centuries earlier.
Medieval Europe was politically fragmented, technologically more limited, and economically less dynamic than Renaissance Europe.
So the nature, pace, and consequences of colonization would likely have been very different.
First, the feasibility of sustained colonization in 1092 is uncertain.
European maritime technology at the end of the 11th century was far less advanced than in the late 15th.
Navigational tools like the magnetic compass were only beginning to spread in Europe.
Atlantic sailing techniques were underdeveloped outside Norse experience.
The Vikings did reach North America around 1000.
But they failed to establish lasting colonies.
European states lacked the naval capacity, population surplus, and centralized financing to support transatlantic ventures.
For colonization in 1092 to succeed, Europe would have needed stronger maritime states earlier or sustained institutional backing.
If such backing had existed, colonization would likely have been slower, smaller in scale, and more decentralized.
Medieval Europe had a much smaller population than in 1492.
Its economy was less commercialized.
Colonies might have resembled frontier outposts or crusader states rather than massive extractive empires.
Feudal structures could have been transplanted across the Atlantic.
Producing semi-autonomous lordships owing allegiance to distant monarchs.
The Church would likely have played a dominant role.
Framing expansion as a missionary enterprise akin to the Crusades.
The most transformative consequence would still have been epidemiological.
Even in 1092, Europeans carried Old World diseases such as smallpox, measles, and influenza.
Indigenous American populations, lacking immunity, would likely have suffered catastrophic declines.
Just as they did after 1492.
However, because medieval Europe had a smaller population and less intense commercial integration, the demographic collapse in the Americas might have unfolded more gradually.
Europe itself would soon face the Black Death in the mid-14th century.
Earlier American contact could have altered disease patterns in both directions.
Though it is uncertain whether major American pathogens would have significantly affected Eurasia.
Economically, Europe in 1092 was not yet positioned to exploit American silver and agricultural wealth on a massive scale.
The price revolution of the 16th century might instead have occurred in the 12th or 13th century.
Potentially accelerating the decline of feudalism and the rise of monetary economies earlier.
Alternatively, limited extraction capacity might have meant that American resources had a muted global impact.
Earlier access to American crops could have boosted European agricultural productivity centuries sooner.
Possibly mitigating famines and reshaping medieval demography.
A more populous Europe before the Black Death might have experienced either a worse pandemic shock or a different recovery trajectory.
Global power balances would also shift.
If Iberian kingdoms or Scandinavian powers had established early American footholds, they might have risen to dominance earlier.
The Islamic world might have responded competitively.
Possibly expanding westward across the Atlantic if knowledge spread.
China’s Song dynasty might have entered transoceanic competition if aware of American lands.
In this scenario, the Americas could have become a contested multipolar frontier rather than predominantly European-controlled.
Most profoundly, Indigenous American civilizations such as the Aztec and Inca empires would not have existed in their later 15th-century forms.
Four centuries earlier, political configurations in Mesoamerica and the Andes were different.
Earlier contact could have interrupted the rise of large centralized empires.
Producing entirely different patterns of alliance, resistance, and cultural exchange.
Some societies might have integrated European technologies gradually rather than facing sudden conquest by gunpowder states.
In sum, colonization beginning in 1092 would likely have been slower, more feudal, and less globally transformative at first.
Over time, it could have accelerated Europe’s economic and political development centuries earlier.
The Columbian Exchange would still have reshaped the world.
But within a medieval framework rather than a Renaissance-capitalist one.
The result might have been an earlier rise of Atlantic-centered power, a restructured medieval world economy, and profoundly altered paths for both European and American civilizations.

items.question: What If Henry dies in the joust and Anne gives birth to a son
human_answers: Judgement Day had finally come for Anne Boleyn. Allies and enemies, alike held their breath when the news broke that King Henry's widow was giving birth. It had been a miracle that she had managed to not miscarry on that fateful January day when her husband had fallen from his horse and would never wake up. When she had learned of Henry's death, Anne had fallen to her knees crying hysterically. However once her tears have passed and she has been calmed down, she immediately summoned the lords to form a regency council, making it clear that she will be regent, a fact that does not sit well with her uncle. Princess Elizabeth would be brought to court, both as a comfort to her mother, and in case she needed to be crowned. Lady Mary was removed from Hatfield and instead put under close guard at Hudson. The Seymours were sent away in disgrace. It was said that Queen Anne took a special delight in dismissing Jane Seymour, mocking her for ever thinking she could replace her. All of Europe held their breath as they waited to see what would happen. Not even the Pope was willing to make a move just yet, wanting to see where the land would lay. Finally on May 19, Anne went into labor. After ten grueling hours, the queen dowager finally brought her second child into the world. "Tis a healthy boy, Majesty, you have done it! You have birthed a prince!" the midwife exclaimed. "Nay, not a prince. A King. I have birthed a King!" Anne cried, a radiant smile on her face. "King Henry the Ninth!"
items.original_question: What if Henry dies in the joust and Anne gives birth to a son Might make this a full TL. Not sure yet. Here is what I am wondering. Let's say that Henry dies and Anne carries her son to term. What happens? Would the people pick Mary when there is chance for a male heir? I know Norfolk and his ilk would probably not turn on Anne when there is a chance that he could be Lord Protector for fifteen years. What about Elizabeth in the meantime, would she be crowned before Anne gives birth just in case Anne gives her a sister?

items.model_answer:
If Henry VIII had died from his jousting accident in January 1536 and Anne Boleyn had subsequently given birth to a healthy son, the immediate result would have been a male Tudor heir—an infant king (effectively Henry IX)—with Anne as queen mother and central figure in the regency government.

Because the boy would have been born to a reigning king and crowned almost immediately after birth, his legitimacy under the 1534 Act of Succession (which recognized Anne’s marriage and invalidated Mary) would have been difficult to challenge legally inside England. However, his position would not have been uncontested. Mary, Henry’s daughter by Catherine of Aragon, still had strong support among conservatives and those loyal to Rome, and Emperor Charles V (her cousin) might have backed her claim diplomatically or even militarily. England could have faced serious factional tension, possibly even rebellion, centered on Mary’s cause.

Domestically, Anne would likely have headed a regency council dominated by reformist figures such as Thomas Cromwell and Thomas Cranmer. Without Henry’s later conservatism and erratic interventions, the English Reformation might have advanced more consistently in a Protestant direction during the 1530s and 1540s. The dissolution of the monasteries would almost certainly have continued, both for ideological and financial reasons. The Church of England might have adopted more explicitly reformist doctrines earlier than it did under Edward VI.

Anne herself would not have fallen in 1536, since the political crisis that destroyed her was tied to her failure to produce a living son and Henry’s desire to remarry. As queen mother to a male heir, her position would have been far stronger, though still vulnerable to factional intrigue. Her survival would also mean no marriage to Jane Seymour and no separate reign of Edward VI; the Protestant succession would be secured through Anne’s son instead.

In the long term, this scenario likely prevents the reigns of both Mary I and Elizabeth I as we know them. Mary’s path to the throne would be blocked by a legitimate male heir, and Elizabeth would remain a secondary princess unless her brother died young. If Anne’s son survived to adulthood, England would probably remain firmly Protestant without the sharp Catholic restoration under Mary or the distinctive Elizabethan religious settlement. The mid-Tudor instability of the 1540s and 1550s might have been reduced—but only if the regency weathered the dangerous early years without civil conflict over the succession.

edus.text: If Henry VIII had died from his jousting accident in January 1536 and Anne Boleyn had subsequently given birth to a healthy son,
the immediate result would have been a male Tudor heir—an infant king (effectively Henry IX)—with Anne as queen mother and central figure in the regency government.
Because the boy would have been born to a reigning king and crowned almost immediately after birth,
his legitimacy under the 1534 Act of Succession (which recognized Anne’s marriage and invalidated Mary) would have been difficult to challenge legally inside England.
However, his position would not have been uncontested.
Mary, Henry’s daughter by Catherine of Aragon, still had strong support among conservatives and those loyal to Rome,
and Emperor Charles V (her cousin) might have backed her claim diplomatically or even militarily.
England could have faced serious factional tension, possibly even rebellion, centered on Mary’s cause.
Domestically, Anne would likely have headed a regency council dominated by reformist figures such as Thomas Cromwell and Thomas Cranmer.
Without Henry’s later conservatism and erratic interventions,
the English Reformation might have advanced more consistently in a Protestant direction during the 1530s and 1540s.
The dissolution of the monasteries would almost certainly have continued, both for ideological and financial reasons.
The Church of England might have adopted more explicitly reformist doctrines earlier than it did under Edward VI.
Anne herself would not have fallen in 1536,
since the political crisis that destroyed her was tied to her failure to produce a living son and Henry’s desire to remarry.
As queen mother to a male heir, her position would have been far stronger,
though still vulnerable to factional intrigue.
Her survival would also mean no marriage to Jane Seymour and no separate reign of Edward VI;
the Protestant succession would be secured through Anne’s son instead.
In the long term, this scenario likely prevents the reigns of both Mary I and Elizabeth I as we know them.
Mary’s path to the throne would be blocked by a legitimate male heir,
and Elizabeth would remain a secondary princess unless her brother died young.
If Anne’s son survived to adulthood,
England would probably remain firmly Protestant without the sharp Catholic restoration under Mary or the distinctive Elizabethan religious settlement.
The mid-Tudor instability of the 1540s and 1550s might have been reduced—
but only if the regency weathered the dangerous early years without civil conflict over the succession.

items.question: What If Britain and France made peace in 1811?
human_answers: I definitely agree that the conflict in Spain would continue, and that some form of renewed conflict in Europe down the line is inevitable, but I don’t think Napoleon wouldn’t try to conclude a peace with Britain, so long as it was on terms favourable to him. Now, whether that is possible is a rather different question. The Whigs at least had no interest in continuing to fund the peninsular war regardless, but in negotiations, they are likely to push for a restoration of Portugal and Hannover, and for France to at least withdraw from direct control of the rest of the Hanseatic cities and the Netherlands. It’s quite a lot for Napoleon to be willing to give up, though could possibly be paired with his longstanding designs on Sicily and a British withdrawal from Malta, as well as the return of occupied Dutch and French colonies. Regardless, I don’t think the British could get everything they want.

No mention has been made of the Continental System. I presume it is abolished as part of the peace treaty. And Britain's blockade is lifted. Anything less makes peace a non starter. Predictions from here: Overall peace is going to be short lived. Every one will be watching France waiting for a propitious moment to reduce the almost total hegemony France has. Nap will maintain a large military to enforce his hegemony. I don't know that this is sustainable. Spain will remain a bleeding ulcer. The Spanish people will continue to resist. Nap's best chance at lasting peace is to pull out and return a Bourbon to power. Remaining in a constant state of this kind of war drains resources, but brings no benefits. The best he can hope for (remaining in the conflict) is an uneasy truce where Joseph is somewhat accepted/propped up, while a low level of guerilla warfare continues. The entire Spanish colonial sphere is lost even faster than OTL. Cuba/puerto rico might remain attached, but I doubt it. I don't know whether Britain has destroyed Spain's infrastructure yet, but if not, Spain could actually emerge from the conflict in better shape without Britain's help than with it. Portugal might be able to hold out behind the line of T, as their soldiers have been trained up to a better level than before 1807, but as the British had supplied the top chain of command, they'll be left rudderless. I think their fate lies in how much stomach Nap has for continuing his Iberian adventure. It would be interesting to see what results if Nap simply walks away. OTL, the British acted as a regency while the Braganza court remained in Brazil. Joao did not want to return. Pedro was too young. Portugal is likely to be chaos. Should France manage to take control, Portugal itself may end up in better shape, but the entirety of the colonial sphere attaches to Brazil. I don't think the return of French colonies does much for France. Haiti is finished as a rich colony. Martinique and Guadeloupe, where Britain ironically enforced the status quo maintaining the slave system after capturing the islands, might still hold value. When the Nap Wars resume, Britain faces a hard choice - join in and try to reset the balance of power, or stay on the sidelines and have the European dynamic dictated to them. If they join in, they're quickly going to regret dropping out in the first place. They had France on the ropes in Portugal/Spain, and now they'll have to start all over again. Who knows what has become of Wellington.

The default of the Revolution certainly left its mark, but Napoleon was also ideologically opposed to debt, in part because of fiscal conservatism (there was a hyperinflation crisis during the Revolution), but also because it would have meant making himself dependent on the financial market, and he feared that the banker would try to exert political pressure on him. But I don't think he necessarily tried to raise a large amount of debt from the public market, he preferred to use a sinking fund controlled by one of his appointees for that. For the reparation, he had ways to force the issue, like sending his army in and making the host pay for its quartering. This was the way he was making his puppets, like the Kingdom of Italy, contribute, and alongside their allied contingent, it saved him as much money as the reparations brought him. For Prussia specifically, they were raising a large debt to pay the reparation, with Napoleon himself being one of their creditors, so they probably intended to pay. But you also have to take into account that Napoleon did not hesitate too much to raise taxes (he essentially brought back every indirect tax of the Ancien Régime) or defer payment, after the Restoration, the Bourbons had to pay the equivalent of one year of fiscal revenues in unpaid expenses.
items.original_question: What if Britain and France made peace in 1811? In 1810 King George III suffered a mental breakdown, and in early 1811, his son the Prince of Wales, later to reign as King George IV, was installed as regent by Parliament. The Prince Regent was widely expected to dismiss Spencer Percival’s government, and appoint Lord Grenville as Prime Minister, but was dissuaded from this course by his mother. Unlike the Tories, Grenville and the Whigs were sceptical of the conflict with France, particularly the expense of maintaining Wellington’s army in the Peninsula War, and had they taken power in 1811, whilst Wellesley’s army was holed up behind the lines of Torres Vedras, attempts at negotiating a peace with France are not an unrealistic prospect. Negotiations in 1807 touted an exchange of Sicily for Hannover, and Britain would retain the Cape Colony and Malta, whilst returning other Dutch and French colonial possessions, though these ultimately broke down over Sicily. Talks in 1808 even saw Napoleon offer to concede both Hannover and Portugal, though there is some question of how serious both sides were in this later negotiation. Both of these were also viewed by the Tory governments as a chance for a respite alike to Amiens, rather than to conclude the conflict. The Whigs, less intractable towards the idea of a French dominated Europe would be willing to pursue a long term peace. In addition to questions over Portugal, Hannover and the colonies though, France had by this point annexed the Netherlands and the Hanseatic cities, both of which are likely to be sticking points for British negotiators (although these annexations were in part to enforce the continental system). What terms could realistically be feasibly agreed by both sides at this time? With the end of the war with Britain in 1811, Napoleon’s invasion of Russia appears unlikely to my mind, though relations between the two emperors would undoubtedly continue to deteriorate. The peace would also presumably be unpopular domestically in Britain, where support for the war remained high. Austria, Prussia and Sweden all additionally had cause to want revenge against France and Napoleon, and so it seems unlikely that this peace would be entirely conclusive, and some form of renewed conflict seems eventually likely, even if it only comes with Bonaparte’s death. The aftermath of Amiens however suggests that this might well come sooner. There is however also the question of whether France could afford to maintain their precarious financial situation, and in particular continue to field their army without the subsides of allies, the reparations of former enemies and loot. It seems unlikely France can afford to demobilise in the face of their European rivals, so would this possibly prompt further campaigns? Perhaps against Russia regardless or the Ottomans?

criteria.name: Counterfactual Premise Integration (Peace in 1811)
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses how well the response incorporates a formal Anglo-French peace in 1811 as a binding premise and adjusts European dynamics accordingly.
criteria.1-2: Ignores or contradicts the 1811 peace premise; continues war as in actual history with minimal adjustment.
criteria.3-4: Mentions peace but leaves major systems (e.g., blockade, Continental System, Peninsular War) unchanged or unexplained.
criteria.5-6: Incorporates peace in some domains (e.g., naval war) but inconsistently applies it across Europe or colonies.
criteria.7-8: Consistently applies the peace settlement to major theaters (Iberia, trade, colonies, diplomacy) with few internal gaps.
criteria.9-10: Fully integrates the 1811 peace as a structural turning point, clearly identifying which policies must end or be renegotiated and tracing systemic adjustments across Europe and the empire.

criteria.name: Causal Mechanism Depth (Political, Economic, Military)
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates the depth and specificity of mechanisms explaining how peace would alter state behavior, alliances, and power balances.
criteria.1-2: Relies on vague assertions (e.g., “things would change”) without mechanisms.
criteria.3-4: Provides limited or single-factor explanations (e.g., only military effects).
criteria.5-6: Explains multiple domains (e.g., trade, military deployments) but with limited detail on how changes unfold.
criteria.7-8: Develops clear multi-step mechanisms linking policy shifts (e.g., lifting blockades) to fiscal, diplomatic, or strategic consequences.
criteria.9-10: Offers detailed, interconnected mechanisms across fiscal systems, alliance structures, military capacity, and imperial governance, showing how changes propagate over time.

criteria.name: Long-Range Chain Coherence (1811 and Beyond)
criteria.criteria_description: Measures how logically and consistently the response traces medium- to long-term consequences beyond the immediate peace.
criteria.1-2: Focuses only on immediate aftermath with no forward projection.
criteria.3-4: Projects forward but with abrupt jumps or contradictions.
criteria.5-6: Provides a plausible sequence of developments but with limited linkage between stages.
criteria.7-8: Constructs a coherent multi-stage trajectory (e.g., Iberia, Russia, colonial systems, future coalitions) with mostly consistent logic.
criteria.9-10: Builds a tightly connected long-range scenario where early changes systematically shape later wars, revolutions, imperial shifts, or balance-of-power realignments.

criteria.name: Coverage of Major Structural Domains
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the response addresses the key arenas implicated by an 1811 peace: Iberian Peninsula, Continental System/blockade, colonial empires, great-power diplomacy (e.g., Russia, Austria, Prussia), and domestic political constraints.
criteria.1-2: Addresses only one minor aspect (e.g., a single battle or leader).
criteria.3-4: Covers one major domain but ignores others central to 1811 geopolitics.
criteria.5-6: Engages at least two major domains but leaves significant blind spots.
criteria.7-8: Covers most major domains with reasonable balance and relevance.
criteria.9-10: Systematically integrates all key domains, showing how developments in one sphere (e.g., trade policy) reshape outcomes in others (e.g., coalition politics or colonial control).

criteria.name: Plausibility, Constraints, and Uncertainty Calibration
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates historical plausibility given 1811 political constraints (e.g., Napoleon’s ambitions, British domestic politics, fiscal limits) and the careful handling of uncertainty.
criteria.1-2: Highly speculative or anachronistic; ignores known constraints of 1811 actors.
criteria.3-4: Some plausibility but overlooks major political or economic constraints.
criteria.5-6: Generally plausible yet occasionally overconfident or insufficiently constrained.
criteria.7-8: Grounds projections in realistic incentives and limits; acknowledges key uncertainties.
criteria.9-10: Demonstrates strong command of 1811 constraints, clearly distinguishes speculation from high-probability outcomes, and avoids internal contradictions while transparently calibrating uncertainty.

items.model_answer:
If Britain and France had made peace in 1811, the trajectory of the Napoleonic Wars—and much of 19th‑century Europe—would likely have changed dramatically.

By 1811 Napoleon dominated continental Europe but was locked in costly struggles: the Peninsular War in Spain and Portugal, economic warfare with Britain through the Continental System, and rising tensions with Russia. A genuine Anglo‑French peace would probably have ended the Peninsular War quickly, since British subsidies and troops were sustaining Iberian resistance. Without Wellington’s army in Portugal and Spain, Napoleon could have withdrawn hundreds of thousands of experienced troops and reduced the financial drain on France.

The most immediate consequence might have been the avoidance—or at least postponement—of Napoleon’s invasion of Russia in 1812. The Continental System existed largely to weaken Britain; if Britain were no longer at war, the rationale for forcing Russia to comply with trade restrictions would disappear. Franco‑Russian tensions would have remained, but without the economic pressure point that drove relations to collapse. Without the catastrophic Russian campaign, Napoleon would have preserved the core of his Grand Army and the aura of invincibility that had kept many European states compliant.

In Britain, peace would have eased economic strain and political unrest caused by trade disruption and war debt. British maritime and colonial dominance would likely have remained intact, since France had little ability to challenge it at sea. Britain might have focused more on imperial expansion overseas, while accepting French predominance on the continent.

For continental Europe, a stable Anglo‑French peace could have consolidated a long-lasting Napoleonic order. Client states such as the Confederation of the Rhine, the Kingdom of Italy, and the Duchy of Warsaw might have endured longer under French hegemony. Austria and Prussia, deprived of British subsidies and the opportunity created by Napoleon’s Russian disaster, would have had little immediate chance to reassert themselves. The nationalist movements in Germany and Spain might have developed more slowly without the galvanizing effect of prolonged war and French defeat.

Over the longer term, however, tensions would likely have resurfaced. Britain and France had fundamentally competing visions of European balance and global trade. Napoleon’s continental dominance and Britain’s naval and financial supremacy were structurally at odds. Even if Napoleon avoided the Russian catastrophe, managing a vast empire dependent on military power and family rule would have been difficult. Internal resistance, economic strains, and succession uncertainties would still have threatened stability.

In short, a peace in 1811 could have prevented Napoleon’s rapid downfall and prolonged French dominance in Europe, possibly delaying the restoration of monarchies and the Concert of Europe. Yet the rivalry between Britain and France, and the internal fragility of Napoleon’s system, suggest that such a peace would more likely have postponed than permanently prevented another major European conflict.

items.question: What If the Mongol Empire had gone to Western Europe instead of the Levant?
human_answers: You are thinking of the Mongol's as a unified force which by this time is not exactly correct. Hulegu and the Ilkhanate were based in Iran (mostly) so the OTL force would not be interested in expanding in Eastern Europe. Batu / Berke and the Golden Horde started their drift towards Islam in this period but their control over the European fringe via their vassals in Kiev and Muscovy wasn't absolute and relied on the tolerance of their Orthodox faith. Any attack on Europe may well become religious in nature (which by itself is an interesting counterfactual) and I suspect any support from the Russian principalities would be lukewarm perhaps even moving towards outright rebellion. It would also be short lived given that the Mongol Civil War is coming. Biggest outcome if the Russian principalities do revolt could be a more Islamised Russia which would be a huge change for world history.

Is there any reason to assume that the forests of western europe were somehow “denser” than those of the eastern? Specifically, those of the Central Russia? BTW, it is not like the Mongols uniformly came from the open steppe: IIRC, Subotai came from Uryankay area which, AFAIK, mostly forests and mountains and he was doing quite well in the Russian forests and pretty much everywhere else. Of course, the Southern direction was much richer than the western one but #1 was the eastern one - China. AFAIK, the South ended up being problematic due to a limited feeding base for the horses but all theories about Mongolian conquest of the west are seemingly ignoring allocation of the resources. The western campaign (including Russia) presumably started with a big force but its second stage, Hungary and Poland, was on a much lesser scale. The map on the OP has “Ulus Jochi” and “Ulus Batu” as separate entities but this was not the case: Batu was a titular head of the Ulus of Jochi. Was there an interest in Mongolia in expanding Ulus Jochi even further at the expense of other endeavors (and other family members)? IMO, this is unlikely because China remained the main theater (BTW, Subotai was sent there after the european campaigns). Were there unlimited human resources? Hardly: part of Hulagu’s force were troops “lended” by Batu. So, with what would Batu conduct his european conquest and why would the Great Khan be interested in its continuation? Formally, the task as formulated by Genghis was fulfilled: the Kipchaks punished and subdued and “the last sea” (Adriatics would do) reached. Was Batu too interested? It does not look like this was a case because he had to create a brand new state from the scratch with the very limited resources (something like 5,000 Mongols).
items.original_question: What if the Mongol Empire had gone to Western Europe instead of the Levant? https://www.reddit.com/r/imaginarymaps/comments/pkb97x/what_if_the_mongols_invaded_europe_the_old_world A sudden interesting thought came to mind. What if, unlike in OTL, the Mongol Empire had not expanded into the Levant and had instead resumed its campaign into Europe? In this TL, during the reign of Möngke Khan, the Mongol Empire invaded Europe again instead of attacking the Abbasid Caliphate. Assume that, starting with the Kingdom of Hungary, they continue pushing westward into the Holy Roman Empire, France, and beyond Western Europe for as long as they keep winning. What I’m curious about is this: 1. What kind of POD would be needed for this to be possible? 2. To what extent would this actually be feasible? - Could the Mongol Empire conquer Western Europe as well, just as it did in Eastern Europe? - Or, unlike in Eastern Europe, would it struggle in Western Europe? 3. If this did happen, what changes would follow? - The Mongol Empire’s advance into Western Europe. - The survival of the Abbasid Caliphate.

items.model_answer:
If the Mongol Empire had concentrated its main expansion on Western Europe rather than turning toward the Levant and the Middle East, the political and cultural trajectory of Europe in the 13th century could have changed dramatically. In reality, the Mongols invaded Eastern and Central Europe in the 1240s, defeating Polish and Hungarian forces, but withdrew after the death of the Great Khan Ögedei. Had they pressed on into Germany, Italy, and France with sustained commitment and reinforcement, Western Europe—then politically fragmented and militarily decentralized—would have faced a profound crisis.

Militarily, Western European kingdoms were divided and often at odds with one another. The Holy Roman Empire was politically fractured, France was consolidating royal power but not yet dominant, and England was preoccupied with its own internal and continental struggles. The Mongols’ mobility, coordination, intelligence networks, and psychological warfare would likely have overwhelmed feudal levies and knight-based armies in open battle, just as they had done in Hungary and Poland. Major cities with strong fortifications might have resisted longer, but without coordinated continental defense, many regions could have fallen into tributary status.

Politically, a successful Mongol penetration into Western Europe might have prevented or delayed the rise of strong centralized monarchies such as Capetian France. Instead of gradual state-building, rulers may have become Mongol vassals, paying tribute in exchange for local autonomy, as happened in parts of Rus’. This could have weakened the papacy’s authority as well. The pope might have attempted to frame resistance as a crusade, but if Rome itself were threatened or subordinated, the ideological leadership of Latin Christendom would have been shaken. Alternatively, the papacy might have pursued diplomatic accommodation, as it did historically by sending envoys to the Mongols.

Economically and culturally, Mongol domination might paradoxically have increased Europe’s integration into Eurasian trade networks earlier and more deeply. Under Mongol rule, the Silk Road flourished. If Western Europe had been securely linked into this system, commercial exchange with China and Central Asia might have accelerated, potentially stimulating technological and scientific transmission earlier than in actual history. However, the destructive phase of conquest would likely have caused massive demographic and urban losses first.

Long term, much would depend on whether Mongol control endured. The Mongol Empire tended to fragment into regional khanates. A “Western Khanate” in Europe might have assimilated, intermarried, and gradually adopted Christianity, as Mongol elites elsewhere adopted Islam or Buddhism. Over generations, this could have produced hybrid ruling elites and altered aristocratic lineages across Europe. On the other hand, if Mongol rule collapsed quickly, Western Europe might have emerged more unified, forged by shared resistance, potentially accelerating political consolidation and military reform.

In short, a sustained Mongol campaign into Western Europe could have delayed or reshaped the rise of centralized monarchies, weakened papal authority, deepened Eurasian integration, and possibly altered the balance between Europe and Asia for centuries. The immediate effects would likely have been devastating, but the long-term consequences would have depended on whether Mongol power proved durable or fragmented as it did elsewhere.

items.question: What If Americans capture Quebec in 1775. How does Quebec's culture & society develop?
human_answers: I can easily see Quebec not wanting to be part of either France, or USA. So they'll opt for independence. France never really wanted it back, so they won't get into their own American Revolution. Even if they did, it is the cost that will impact the French Revolution. The cost will add to French woes. This notion that France will rise up in revolution because Quebec wants independence is erroneous. France wanted regime/gov't change, which is not at all what Quebec wants (independence). France will add Quebec to the list of grievances. That does NOT make Quebec the birthplace of this alt FR. There were various causes of the ARW. One of them was putting Ohio under Canadian jurisdiction. Plus the French and Indian War was fought over the Ohio Valley, and led to a lot of the grievances leading to ARW. No one considers Ohio the birthplace of the AR. Semantics? maybe, but I don't think so.

It is difficult to ascertain how the French in Canada felt, as they lived in a quasi-medieval subsistence economy. Although not under full-blown feudalism, their society was paternalistic, hierarchical, and agrarian. The Church and the seigneurs (many of the seigneuries were owned by religious orders) were the pillars of authority. This is crucial in explaining the lack of widespread revolutionary fervour. However, in the late eighteenth century, there remained a cultural and sentimental connection to France, particularly to the Ancien Régime and the monarchy. After the executions of Louis XVI and Marie Antoinette, masses were said for them, and the French press in Quebec noted this. They were mourning the grandson of their last French sovereign, not celebrating the secular republic that executed him. In December 1778, from Boston, French Admiral d’Estaing called on the Canadiens to rise and rejoin their motherland, but this was difficult as Canada was where most British forces were stationed. It is unclear whether they wished to return to France, but the Continental Congress felt uneasy about the French returning to North America. Because the Canadiens were largely illiterate (literacy was still below 40% in 1850), it is difficult to say whether they were politically sophisticated, as the colony had been largely marginal and lacked a large merchant class under French rule. Education was not widespread and was largely controlled by seminaries or convents. It was even less politically sophisticated than the Spanish colonies in the Americas. My guess is that independence would have been the least likely of options, unless the Bishop of Quebec assumed the role of head of government.

Then the place will find a way to get out of American control ASAP. Mismatched expectations and all that because of a fundamental misreading by the Continental Army/Congress of the situation, particularly WRT the Quebec Act. The French never wanted to retain Canada après la Conquête because the sugar colonies in the Caribbean were far more valuable, plus lots of bad blood between the Canadiens and Versailles about which direction their part of New France should go. You'd basically be accelerating the French Revolution's TL but with a Canadien cause - and this time the British would come off as the good guys by allying with the habitants, whether or not it takes it back under its wing or accepts it as an independent country but under the British sphere of influence. And it finds a way to get out of the US ASAP, particularly if the initial military occupation goes as OTL and they basically alienated everyone. More probable than getting annexed by the US. Considering Quebec in this case would be a direct cause for the French Revolution ITTL, that's easy to remark on. While still predominantly Francophone (albeit with Canadian French given the same recognition as, say, Brazilian Portuguese), society and culture would take a more, say, Argentine or Uruguayan-like direction but w/ its own quirks (including probably far more indigenous influence) and probably different relationships among groups that would be relatively more egalitarian and opposed to reinstating the colonial relationship. Considering the British would still be next door viz. Newfoundland and Nova Scotia, as well as the HBC doing its thing, British influence would remain strong and that would include the cultural sphere, too.

It depends on how the Americans treat the Canadiens, and how they handle the Iroquois. If the Americans can't keep the Iroquois mostly neutral, and if they prevent them from trading with the Canadiens, then Quebec will want want to leave in a hurry. If the Americans could be deft in the administration of Quebec, better in battle, luckier with allied victories, and more skillful in peace negotiation I think there is a good chance that the Canadiens would want to be in a confederacy, or a customs union with a mutual defense pact. The centralizing reforms of the Constitution would likely have been opposed by the Canadiens as antifederalism, which brings me to the next point, though it is possible they could remain in the union if it transitions from Articles of Confederation to Constitution. While the Canadiens would most likely have forbade slavery, that doesn't mean they would have been abolitionists in the vein of the northeastern Calvinists and Quakers. While they could have been like the 1840s and 1850s Free Soilers, their antifederalism and relative lack of industrialization might have moved them into common cause with Southern states. The Canadiens also could have been aligned with the "Westerners" in looking for federally funded internal developments to help with their access to Atlantic ports, and their access to settling Upper Canada and Indiana/Illinois Territory. Being so close to Nova Scotia and Newfoundland the Canadiens could also be interested in a strong navy. So perhaps an American Quebec could be allied with someone like Calhoun. As for the issue of Loyalist Migration, their emigration would likely have been reduced if they didn't have British Upper Canada as a destination. Many of the Loyalists would have resigned themselves to life in the new government. There still would have been Loyalist emigration from both America and Lower Canada, and there would still be a movement of Loyalists to Upper Canada and other territories despite them being no longer British Empire owned. So those populations would have thrown a new political impulse into the country later especially after the Constitution is ratified.

I'd assume a French route with independence after the French revolution. Maybe some nobility or rich flee to Quebec during the revolution. I'd think US keeps what it would get otl plus Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Prince Edward island. Ontario might go to the U.S. While Newfoundland and Labrador goes to Quebec. The American loyalists could be moved into western Canada to try to colonize Western Canada. England might be more harsh in dealing with the Oregon territory. You could see a war over it with Quebec siding with a side. Should U.S. Win they might get British Columbia in the treaty. Quebec might get islands in Nunavut. Russia in this timeline would probably favor selling Alaska to England. With more northern territory. I can see the South looking for more Mexican territory. There's a possibility the slave and free state addition could continue on longer. This causes a delay of the civil war potentially.
items.original_question: What if Americans capture Quebec in 1775. How does Quebec's culture & society develop? So having just watched a new video from Blue, it gave me an idea of dusting off an old topic I used to talk about In 1775, the Continental Army under Generals, Richard Montgomery, Daniel Morgan, James Livingston, and Benedict Arnold (Yes, that Benedict Arnold) marched north into Canada in an attempt to capture Quebec from the British and persuade the French Canadians in joining the revolution. It went well for part of the expedition at first, with Montgomery nearly capturing British Govenor Guy Carleton in Montreal. Meanwhile Arnold's part journeyed through the wilderness to get to Quebec City, which was very difficult. However, by the time the Americans gotten to Quebec, a snowstorm occurred and the battle turned into an utter disaster. Montgomery got killed, Arnold was wounded, smallpox plagued the Americans, the British suffered few causalities, and the Americans managed to alienate the Canadians. Meanwhile, Carleton received reinforcements and made a counter offensive that drove the Americans back to Fort Ticonderoga. For context, what if the Americans captured Quebec? Say Montgomery captured Govenor Guy Carleton and the Americans managed to catch Quebec City by surprise. In my previous thread about the fate of Quebec (Roughly around Lower Canada; Upper Canada is a whole other can of worms), there were four possibilities I gave, but we're going to talk about three: A) French route- The Americans offer Quebec back to France for support in their war, meaning France regains Quebec by the end of the war B) American route- The Americans annex Quebec, making Quebec part of the USA. C) Independent route- The Americans make Quebec into a sister republic, making Quebec independent by the end of the war. (There's no British route since that OTL) Now, I want to focus on one particular aspect of the fate of Quebec: Culture. If Quebec wasn't under the British/TTL Canada, what would culture be like for the French Canadians. Depending on the route we take, how would culture, society, art, cuisine, fashion, etc, develop for the French Canadians? In the French route, how would Quebec be affected by the French Revolution? In the American route, how would Quebec develop under the USA? In the Independent route, how would Quebec develop stuck between the British and Americans while having access to the St Lawrence?

items.model_answer:
If American forces had successfully captured and held Quebec in 1775–76, the province’s cultural and social development would likely have diverged sharply from the path it followed under British rule. The most important shift would have been from becoming the core of French Canadian survival within the British Empire to becoming a francophone minority region inside a new American republic.

In the short term, the Continental Congress would almost certainly have tried to honor its earlier promises to French Canadians: protection of Catholicism, continuation of French civil law, and local autonomy. Congress had already appealed to Quebec’s inhabitants in 1774–75 by criticizing Britain’s Quebec Act but also by promising representative government. To secure loyalty in wartime, the Americans likely would have allowed Catholic worship and retained elements of French civil law, at least initially. However, unlike the British Empire after 1774, the United States had no strong institutional commitment to preserving French legal and cultural autonomy over the long term.

Politically, Quebec would probably have entered the Union as one or more states, perhaps divided along the St. Lawrence valley. Early statehood would have required an elected assembly and integration into American federal structures. This would have accelerated the introduction of English-language political culture, common law influences, and Protestant Anglo-American settlers. Land tenure under the seigneurial system might have been gradually dismantled in favor of American-style private property norms, particularly as migration from New England and New York increased.

Demographically, the impact could have been transformative. Under British rule, French Canadians remained an overwhelming majority in Lower Canada well into the 19th century. Within the United States, migration pressures would likely have been far stronger. New Englanders moving north into the fertile St. Lawrence valley, combined with westward expansion routes running through the region, could have made francophones a shrinking proportion of the population by the early or mid-19th century. The cultural balance might have come to resemble Louisiana: a historically French society that retained elements of language and civil law but gradually became Anglicized and integrated into a broader American identity.

Religion would have been another key factor. The United States’ constitutional separation of church and state would have prevented the kind of formal church-state partnership that helped structure Quebec society under British rule. The Catholic Church would have remained influential locally, but without state-backed privileges or a British imperial policy designed to secure Catholic loyalty. Over time, Protestant denominations would likely have grown with Anglo-American settlement, weakening the near-monopoly the Catholic Church held in 19th-century Quebec.

National identity would also have evolved differently. In real history, French Canadian identity solidified partly in opposition to British institutions and later to Anglo-Protestant dominance within Canada. If Quebec had been American from the revolutionary era onward, its inhabitants might have developed a dual identity: culturally French but politically American, similar to how many ethnic groups in the United States retained cultural distinctiveness while embracing civic nationalism. Movements for linguistic preservation might have emerged, but probably without the same state-centered nationalism that later fueled Quebecois separatism. There would be no Confederation in 1867 to rally against, and no Canadian federal framework within which Quebec could claim founding-nation status.

Internationally, the capture of Quebec would also have altered continental geopolitics. Without a British-controlled Canada, there would have been less incentive for Loyalists to migrate north, reducing the development of an English-speaking Ontario as a counterweight to French Quebec. The entire northern tier of North America might have become American much earlier, further embedding Quebec within a predominantly English-speaking republic.

Overall, Quebec under American control would likely have experienced stronger demographic and linguistic assimilation pressures. French language and civil law traditions might have survived regionally—especially if protected early on—but the long-term trajectory would probably resemble partial integration rather than the sustained, institutionally supported distinct society that developed within Canada. Quebec would still be culturally marked by its French origins, but it would be far less politically and nationally distinct than it became in Canadian history.

edus.text: If American forces had successfully captured and held Quebec in 1775–76, the province’s cultural and social development would likely have diverged sharply from the path it followed under British rule.
The most important shift would have been from becoming the core of French Canadian survival within the British Empire to becoming a francophone minority region inside a new American republic.

In the short term, the Continental Congress would almost certainly have tried to honor its earlier promises to French Canadians: protection of Catholicism, continuation of French civil law, and local autonomy.
Congress had already appealed to Quebec’s inhabitants in 1774–75 by criticizing Britain’s Quebec Act but also by promising representative government.
To secure loyalty in wartime, the Americans likely would have allowed Catholic worship and retained elements of French civil law, at least initially.
However, unlike the British Empire after 1774, the United States had no strong institutional commitment to preserving French legal and cultural autonomy over the long term.
Politically, Quebec would probably have entered the Union as one or more states, perhaps divided along the St. Lawrence valley.
Early statehood would have required an elected assembly and integration into American federal structures.
This would have accelerated the introduction of English-language political culture, common law influences, and Protestant Anglo-American settlers.
Land tenure under the seigneurial system might have been gradually dismantled in favor of American-style private property norms, particularly as migration from New England and New York increased.
Demographically, the impact could have been transformative.
Under British rule, French Canadians remained an overwhelming majority in Lower Canada well into the 19th century.
Within the United States, migration pressures would likely have been far stronger.

New Englanders moving north into the fertile St. Lawrence valley, combined with westward expansion routes running through the region, could have made francophones a shrinking proportion of the population by the early or mid-19th century.

The cultural balance might have come to resemble Louisiana: a historically French society that retained elements of language and civil law but gradually became Anglicized and integrated into a broader American identity.
Religion would have been another key factor.
The United States’ constitutional separation of church and state would have prevented the kind of formal church-state partnership that helped structure Quebec society under British rule.
The Catholic Church would have remained influential locally, but without state-backed privileges or a British imperial policy designed to secure Catholic loyalty.
Over time, Protestant denominations would likely have grown with Anglo-American settlement, weakening the near-monopoly the Catholic Church held in 19th-century Quebec.
National identity would also have evolved differently.
In real history, French Canadian identity solidified partly in opposition to British institutions and later to Anglo-Protestant dominance within Canada.

If Quebec had been American from the revolutionary era onward, its inhabitants might have developed a dual identity: culturally French but politically American, similar to how many ethnic groups in the United States retained cultural distinctiveness while embracing civic nationalism.
Movements for linguistic preservation might have emerged, but probably without the same state-centered nationalism that later fueled Quebecois separatism.
There would be no Confederation in 1867 to rally against, and no Canadian federal framework within which Quebec could claim founding-nation status.
Internationally, the capture of Quebec would also have altered continental geopolitics.
Without a British-controlled Canada, there would have been less incentive for Loyalists to migrate north, reducing the development of an English-speaking Ontario as a counterweight to French Quebec.
The entire northern tier of North America might have become American much earlier, further embedding Quebec within a predominantly English-speaking republic.
Overall, Quebec under American control would likely have experienced stronger demographic and linguistic assimilation pressures.

French language and civil law traditions might have survived regionally—especially if protected early on—but the long-term trajectory would probably resemble partial integration rather than the sustained, institutionally supported distinct society that developed within Canada.
Quebec would still be culturally marked by its French origins, but it would be far less politically and nationally distinct than it became in Canadian history.

items.question: Administration of British colonies in North America if the USA would have never existed?
human_answers: With this POD, Spain and, especially, France may have a very different trajectory from 1776. Both have been looking for a way to get back at Britain for the disastrous 7YW. ARW provided that way, OTL. That involvement did 2 things (more than that, but)...it waylaid the slow progress Spain was making up the Pacific Coast, and most importantly, helped set the stage for the French Revolution. There will be another war. Maybe the WoBavarian Succession spins out of control. Maybe Britain decides to assist Portugal in its struggles against Spain in mid-late 1770s, and this spins out of control. Maybe one or the other leaves the path to the French Revolution still on track. Or, maybe the wars are delayed, and FR as we know it is butterflied. That is beyond BIG. And, this all assumes that the colonies remain at peace, not rising up for round 2, or 3. During the Nootka Crisis, Spain looked to France for assistance, which it didn't get because of the FR. Plus, throughout the 18th century, France didn't go to Spain's aid, but, rather, expected it to be the other way around. I wouldn't count on France backing Spain in the Nootka Crisis, even if there was no FR. If left by its lonesome, Spain likely backs down as OTL. Or maybe Spain has used the decade or 2 of peace to continue settling the Pacific north coast.

I guess if England would have kept the economically important and more or less developed 13C it would have a smaller interest in Notka/Oregon/access to the pacific. If the ARW ends in 1775/1776 then yes, Spain would have had more time and resources to actually colonize Notka. To be honest, I never understood why so many people believe that with a failed ARW, the French R. simply never happens. France was still economically and politically and socially in a bad situation. So yeah, I think the FR still would have happened. Maybe sooner or later (most likely a bit later) and maybe less bloody, but IMO it still would have happened nonetheless. And yeah, France and Spain still would have tried to get revenge on England. How realistic is that if the ARW ends in 1775/1776? I mean the whole American mythos of Americans rising up against the british crown is not that true. A lot of American colonists were loyal to the crown. Its not that every peasant in the 13C rose up against George III and with that rebellion or uprising put down quickly, I think the motivation for another rebellion would be low. How realistic is a peaceful solution to the pacific question? So England keeps the 13C and let's say that that James Cook dies earlier so there is no English expedition at the pacific coast and England has less information and is less interested in these regions. And if Spain has more time, money to colonize Notka could England have decided to just let Spain have it?
items.original_question: Administration of British colonies in North America if the USA would have never existed? I have seen several maps of North America in alternate history scenarios where the 13 colonies lost in 1775/1776. IF England would have won, how would they have administered their colonies in North America afterwards in the late 18th, the 19th, and the 20th century? Would they have administered their colonies separately (Pensilvania, Massachusetts, Newfoundland, Quebec, "Canada?", Florida, Louisiana, Oregon etc.) or would they have united them sooner or later in a big north american british dominion? Also, would they have eventually taken oregon/nootka? what about louisiana and alaska from france and russia respectively? PS: Yes I know there are a lot of "What if the US lost the war of 1776..." threads here but this is mostly about the administration of these colonies

items.model_answer:
If the United States had never come into existence—meaning the American Revolution either failed or never occurred—the British colonies in North America would likely have remained within the British Empire and evolved along lines similar to Canada, Australia, and New Zealand.

In the short term, Britain would have continued tightening imperial administration after the Seven Years’ War. The imperial reforms that sparked colonial resistance—taxation measures, trade regulation, and stronger royal oversight—would likely have been implemented more gradually or negotiated into a more federated imperial system. London may have granted the colonies greater parliamentary representation or expanded colonial self-government to prevent unrest, much as it later did in white settler colonies.

Over the nineteenth century, British North America would probably have consolidated into one or more large self-governing dominions. The Thirteen Colonies might have been reorganized alongside Canada into a federated “Dominion of North America,” with responsible government, a local parliament, and autonomy over domestic affairs while foreign policy and defense remained under British control. This mirrors the path Canada followed after 1867.

Westward expansion would likely still have occurred, but under tighter imperial management. British policy before 1776 aimed to regulate settlement beyond the Appalachians to stabilize relations with Indigenous nations. Without U.S. independence and its aggressive land speculation and expansionist ideology, westward growth may have been slower, more centralized, and more treaty-based—though still ultimately expansionist, as seen in Canada and Australia.

Slavery would probably have been abolished earlier than it was in the United States. The British Empire abolished slavery in 1833. In a British North America that included the southern colonies, slavery might have ended at that time across the continent, potentially avoiding a civil war like the American Civil War. However, this would have required managing strong planter resistance, particularly in colonies such as Virginia and South Carolina.

Politically, the region would likely have evolved into a parliamentary system under a constitutional monarchy rather than a presidential republic. There would be no U.S. Constitution as we know it; instead, governance would follow the Westminster model with a prime minister, cabinet government, and a governor-general representing the Crown.

Globally, the absence of an independent United States would have significantly altered power balances. Britain might have remained the dominant North Atlantic power longer, supported by a vast and unified North American dominion. The French Revolution and Napoleonic Wars would still have occurred, but without a U.S. republic as a political model. In the twentieth century, a British-led North America would likely have entered world wars as part of the Empire/Commonwealth, similar to Canada but on a much larger scale.

In summary, if the United States had never existed, British North America would most plausibly have developed into one or more large self-governing dominions within the British Empire—politically similar to Canada but territorially vast—featuring parliamentary government, earlier empire-wide abolition of slavery, more gradual constitutional evolution, and continued cultural and institutional ties to Britain.

items.question: What If the Southern Ming had survived?
human_answers: I foresee a successful Chinese expedition to retake the North within a decade or two. Sichuan was perhaps ironically where the most effective anti-Qing forces were based in OTL. Remnants of Zhang Xianzhong and Li Zicheng’s forces continued fighting there for decades until well into Kangxi’s reign IOTL. The site saw repeated struggles between different forces for many decades. It’s actually the reason for the significant decline in the population of Sichuan IOTL, not Zhang Xianzhong’s Sichuan massacre. Population wise, the Qing Dynasty would have difficulty regrowing the population of the north due to lack of food. The North has always been a basket case since the end of the Northern Song Dynasty. During the Ming Dynasty, Southern China had at least two times the population of the North. And that is before the collapse of the Ming Dynasty Which saw massive fighting. You see plenty of areas throughout Northern China eating rice as staples today, but the truth was that this is evidence for how much northerners have come to rely on Southern grain. Rice does not grow in the North, and has to be imported from the South. Before the Sui-Tang Dynasties when the Grand Canal was not built, Northern diet was based on wheat. Still is to a lesser extent today. After this period, they became increasingly reliant on Southern crops until from the Ming Dynasty onwards, they became entirely reliant on it. Northern Qing can’t just regrow when they don’t even have the rice to feed the people. As time goes on, even by the 17th century, warfare is gonna increasingly dependant upon firearms, meaning population,technology and economy is gonna become decisive in eventual Southern victory. Individual prowess of the troops that the Manchus relied heavily on will become less relevant,especially as the Qing simply does not have Manchu population to supply large armies to both stamp out rebellions or to fight the Southern dynasty. The Manchus iotl exploited a critical window before that was gonna be a problem to conquer the South.

This is what I have in mind: 1. In OTL, as I understand it, by this point the Ming dynasty’s North China had been devastated, the population had grown unevenly, and the state had come to depend heavily on Jiangnan’s grain resources. In that situation, if the Qing were to occupy only North China while the Ming retained control of Jiangnan, the Qing would likely suffer from serious food shortages. Under such conditions, I think it is highly likely that the Qing would resort to massacres in North China similar to the Yangzhou massacre seen in OTL. However, in the end, the Qing might later face the problem of overpopulation once again. Personally, when it comes to the Malthusian trap, I think the Northern Qing would suffer from it more severely than the Southern Ming. What do you think? 2. In OTL, the Dzungars were destroyed by Qing expeditions. However, in this timeline, the Dzungars would likely expand their power significantly across Mongolia and Tibet. Unlike in OTL, the Qing would probably remain largely on the defensive. As a result, the Dzungars would not be destroyed and would likely enjoy a substantial imperial existence until they were eventually conquered by the Russian Empire. Russia, too, would likely push into Manchuria more frequently and more deeply than it did in OTL. The Qing would have a much harder time containing them and would probably have to request military assistance from Joseon more often than in OTL . It is even possible that, unlike the Treaty of Nerchinsk, Russia might succeed in extracting territorial gains much deeper inside the region. And here is the next question. In your view, assuming that the Southern Ming and the Northern Qing both survived until the mid-18th century, which state do you think would collapse first? And in what ways do you think each polity would face its respective crises? First of all, in OTL, the course of the Yellow River changed in the 1850s. This could also have significant effects on China.

Why do you say they will sinicise faster? By contrast, I think they’d sinicise even slower, as they can’t hope to match the southern Ming in chineseness and so would have to rely on other pillars of legitimacy to prop up their rule, perhaps leaning further into Tibetan Buddhism. Edit- looking more into how Tibetan Buddhism had spread so deeply into Mongol society in the late 16th century, people seem to say that the Qing need to appeal to Taoist and Confucian ideologies meant they could not be called a primarily Buddhist state. Ittl, I think the Qing would lean much more heavily into buddhist kingship, and this might also make their policy towards Han people less racist- there would be a way for Han people to politically abandon the Confucian-Taoist kingship embodied by the Ming, by adopting Tibetan Buddhism, which would make them part of the ruling group without becoming Manchu. Why do you say it didn’t happen in India? As an aside, there was a mid 17th century equivalent to the treaty of Westphalia in Central Asia, the Great Code of 1640, by which various Oirat and Mongol clans agreed to act as a collective body to uphold general peace and a universal legal code, while upholding the sovereignty of the individual tribes. Otl, it became irrelevant once the Qing got rid of any form of Mongol sovereignty by defeating the Dzunghars and winning the Khalkha Mongols to their cause, but in a world where the Qing aren’t so powerful, the “Holy Mongol Empire” likely maintains its constitutional structure for longer. Instead of a Dzunghar khanate, we’d therefore talk Ming China allying with the Western Yuan Dynasty to hold back the Qing, and perhaps the federal Yuan would be more successful than the Dzunghar were otl in their wars against the Kazakhs/the Khanates of Bukhara. Or perhaps, the Qing end up functioning as the Austria analogue- personally controlling by far the most land and people, but still unable to strip away the autonomy of the various Mongol and oirat ulus’, who regularly meet and would all revolt against imperial overreach.
items.original_question: If the Southern Ming had survived? Thread 'Perpetual Brightness: Surviving Southern Ming' Apr 12, 2006 Once, the Confucian school outside Quanzhou had bustled with students and scholars. Some of China’s greatest administrators had come from there, and in its day the school had been a center of learning. But since the famines, and the Manchu invasion, the school had grown quiet. The buildings were dilapidated, with peeling paint and rotten timber. There was only one man there, in the dark of night, standing by a fire. The man watched as the flames cast a red glow over the temple, as it consumed the robes of a scholar. An Empire was collapsing outside its walls, but inside the silence was... Faeelin Replies: 168 Forum: Alternate History Discussion: Before 1900 In OTL, after an empire collapsed in China, there were many cases where it was not completely destroyed and replaced by another empire, but instead split into northern and southern regimes. Even before the Qing dynasty, the Jurchen states themselves formed a northern empire, while the Southern Song continued to exist in the south. In the 17th century, the Ming dynasty, like the Song before it, also established the Southern Ming. However, it ultimately fell after only twenty years. Was there no way for the Southern Ming to survive? The problems of the Southern Ming, as I see them, are as follows. 1. In the case of the Southern Song, all other imperial claimants were captured by the Jurchens, and as a result, a person low in the line of succession became the only remaining claimant. This, paradoxically, allowed him to secure a certain degree of legitimacy and take power. By contrast, the Southern Ming began in a situation where the legitimate imperial princes had largely been captured from the outset, while there were still too many lower-ranking imperial relatives remaining. This excess of potential claimants triggered disputes over the imperial succession. 2. In the case of the Jin dynasty, it had not yet fully subdued the Western Xia or the Mongols. In particular, the Mongols were later unified by Genghis Khan, who went on to establish the most powerful nomadic empire in history. At the time, the Goryeo dynasty was nominally a tributary state of the Jin, but it had not been decisively subdued through war. The Jin lacked the capacity to invade Goryeo and had no choice but to settle for maintaining relatively moderate relations. In other words, the Jin dynasty could not devote all of its national strength to the conquest of the Southern Song. By contrast, the Qing dynasty had already conquered the Chahar Mongols and had invaded the capital of the Joseon dynasty, forcing it into clear submission. Although the Dzungars and Russia would later enter the Chinese arena, this occurred only after the game had effectively already been decided. 3. The Southern Song was able to survive thanks to outstanding generals such as Yue Fei and Han Shizhong, who successfully defeated the Jurchen armies. By contrast, on the eve of the Ming dynasty’s collapse, Wu Sangui’s forces—virtually the only remaining elite army—defected outright to the Qing side. As a result, the Southern Ming was forced to struggle on with inadequate military strength, trapped in a situation where incompetent warlords fought among themselves in constant internal conflict. Taking these factors into account, I think that for the Southern Ming to have survived for a long time, things would have had to be different from the very beginning. “Before the fall of Beijing, the Chongzhen Emperor decides to transfer the capital to Nanjing. Abandoning Beijing, he withdraws south, and Wu Sangui’s army joins the emperor’s entourage and moves to Nanjing as well.” In effect, this would mean that the Chongzhen Emperor is “ceding North China to the Jurchens,” but even so, the southern regions would be far more securely preserved. However, he did not do so. The reasons lie here. In short, he was an “indecisive and irresolute emperor,” and as a result, instead of taking responsibility for such a momentous decision, he merely kept postponing it. What I am curious about is this: 1. If the Chongzhen Emperor were to decide on relocating the capital, what kind of POD (point of divergence) would need to occur? 2. If the Southern Ming had survived at least until the 19th century, how would East Asian history from the 17th to the 19th centuries have changed? Assuming the Southern Ming succeeded in repelling the initial Qing offensives, who would be in the more advantageous position thereafter? If the Southern Ming were to endure, how would Western powers in the 19th century approach China?

items.model_answer:
If the Southern Ming had survived, the most immediate consequence would have been a divided China, much like the earlier Northern–Southern dynasties or the Song–Jin period. Rather than the Qing unifying the empire under Manchu rule, China might have stabilized into a north–south political split, with the Qing controlling North China and the Southern Ming entrenched in the Yangzi basin and the maritime southeast. Over time, either coexistence or prolonged warfare would have defined East Asian geopolitics.

For the Southern Ming to survive, it would have needed to consolidate leadership, suppress factionalism, and effectively coordinate loyalist generals such as Zheng Chenggong (Koxinga). If it achieved this, the lower Yangzi region—already the economic heartland of China—would have given it significant fiscal strength. Control of maritime trade through Fujian, Guangdong, and connections to Southeast Asia and Japan would have further enriched the regime. A Southern Ming state might therefore have become more commercially and maritime oriented than the land-focused Qing, potentially accelerating naval development and overseas engagement.

The political character of China would also have shifted. The Qing introduced the banner system, preserved Manchu identity, and later oversaw territorial expansion into Inner Asia (Xinjiang, Mongolia, Tibet). A surviving Southern Ming likely would have lacked the military capacity and political motivation for such expansive Inner Asian conquests. As a result, the territorial boundaries of “China” might have been smaller and more Han-centered, possibly excluding or only loosely influencing regions like Xinjiang or Tibet. Inner Asia could have remained under independent Mongol, Oirat, or other steppe polities.

Culturally, the absence of Qing rule would have meant no queue order, no large-scale Manchu–Han integration policies, and no Kangxi–Qianlong high Qing synthesis. Neo-Confucian orthodoxy would likely have continued, but under the stress of survival, the Southern Ming might have encouraged more practical statecraft reforms. Loyalist literati, who historically became critics and scholars under Qing rule, might instead have shaped a reforming Ming court. Intellectual currents such as evidential scholarship might have emerged differently or later.

Foreign relations would also have diverged. The Qing managed relations with Russia, Central Asia, and Tibet from a position as a continental empire. A Southern Ming, more maritime and commercially exposed, would have faced European expansion—especially Dutch, Spanish, and later British—under different circumstances. If strong at sea, it might have negotiated from a position of greater parity in the 17th and 18th centuries. Alternatively, internal weakness could have made it more vulnerable to European naval pressure earlier than the Qing were.

In the long term, the biggest difference may have been symbolic and national. The Qing’s status as a non-Han dynasty later fed narratives of “foreign conquest” in modern Chinese nationalism. A surviving Ming would have preserved uninterrupted Han dynastic rule, potentially altering modern nationalist identity. The revolutionary rhetoric of the 19th and early 20th centuries—often framed against Manchu rule—might never have taken the same form.

Overall, a surviving Southern Ming would likely have produced a China that was more southern, maritime, commercially oriented, and possibly territorially smaller. East Asia might have seen a prolonged Sino-Manchu duality or an eventual Ming reconquest. In either case, the political, cultural, and territorial shape of modern China would have been significantly different.

Rather than the Qing unifying the empire under Manchu rule, China might have stabilized into a north–south political split.
The Qing would have controlled North China and the Southern Ming would have been entrenched in the Yangzi basin and the maritime southeast.
Over time, either coexistence or prolonged warfare would have defined East Asian geopolitics.
For the Southern Ming to survive, it would have needed to consolidate leadership, suppress factionalism, and effectively coordinate loyalist generals such as Zheng Chenggong (Koxinga).
If it achieved this, the lower Yangzi region would have given it significant fiscal strength.
The lower Yangzi region was already the economic heartland of China.
Control of maritime trade through Fujian, Guangdong, and connections to Southeast Asia and Japan would have further enriched the regime.
A Southern Ming state might therefore have become more commercially and maritime oriented than the land-focused Qing.
This orientation might have accelerated naval development and overseas engagement.
The political character of China would also have shifted.
The Qing introduced the banner system, preserved Manchu identity, and later oversaw territorial expansion into Inner Asia.
A surviving Southern Ming likely would have lacked the military capacity and political motivation for such expansive Inner Asian conquests.
As a result, the territorial boundaries of China might have been smaller and more Han-centered.
Regions like Xinjiang or Tibet might have been excluded or only loosely influenced.
Inner Asia could have remained under independent Mongol, Oirat, or other steppe polities.
Culturally, the absence of Qing rule would have meant no queue order, no large-scale Manchu–Han integration policies, and no Kangxi–Qianlong high Qing synthesis.
Neo-Confucian orthodoxy would likely have continued.
Under the stress of survival, the Southern Ming might have encouraged more practical statecraft reforms.
Loyalist literati might have shaped a reforming Ming court.
Intellectual currents such as evidential scholarship might have emerged differently or later.
Foreign relations would also have diverged.
The Qing managed relations with Russia, Central Asia, and Tibet from a position as a continental empire.
A Southern Ming would have faced European expansion under different circumstances.
If strong at sea, it might have negotiated from a position of greater parity.
Alternatively, internal weakness could have made it more vulnerable to European naval pressure earlier than the Qing were.
In the long term, the biggest difference may have been symbolic and national.
The Qing’s status as a non-Han dynasty fed narratives of foreign conquest in modern Chinese nationalism.
A surviving Ming would have preserved uninterrupted Han dynastic rule.
This might have altered modern nationalist identity.
Revolutionary rhetoric framed against Manchu rule might never have taken the same form.
Overall, a surviving Southern Ming would likely have produced a China that was more southern, maritime, commercially oriented, and possibly territorially smaller.
East Asia might have seen a prolonged Sino-Manchu duality or an eventual Ming reconquest.
In either case, the political, cultural, and territorial shape of modern China would have been significantly different.
