items.model_answer:
If the Austrian Netherlands (roughly modern Belgium and Luxembourg) had been partitioned in the 18th century, the consequences would have depended on who divided it and when, but the overall trajectory of Western Europe would likely have shifted in several important ways.

The most plausible moment for partition would have been during the War of the Austrian Succession (1740–1748) or earlier during the War of the Spanish Succession (1701–1714). France had long sought to push its northeastern frontier to more defensible “natural borders,” while the Dutch Republic wanted buffer fortresses against French expansion. Prussia or other German states might also have pressed claims in Luxembourg or Liège. If Austria had lost control and the territory had been divided primarily between France and the Dutch (or smaller German states), the strategic buffer between France and the Dutch Republic would have been permanently altered.

If France had annexed most or all of the Austrian Netherlands in the mid-18th century, it would have gained economically advanced, densely populated, and industrially promising regions decades before the French Revolutionary Wars. This would have strengthened France financially and militarily before 1789. The French Revolutionary expansion into Belgium in the 1790s would not have been necessary, and the ideological export of revolution into the Low Countries might have been more limited or taken a different form. A pre-revolutionary annexation could also have reduced one of the Revolutionary Wars’ key theaters, possibly altering coalition dynamics.

If instead the region had been partitioned among smaller powers—say, France taking Flanders, the Dutch taking frontier fortresses, and parts going to German states—the area might have become fragmented like western Germany. In that case, no unified Belgian state would likely have emerged in 1830. The Belgian Revolution depended in part on the territory’s prior administrative unity under Austrian and then French rule. Without that unity, a coherent Belgian national identity might never have formed, and the territory might today be divided between France, the Netherlands, and Germany or Luxembourg.

Strategically, an earlier French annexation would have alarmed Britain. Britain consistently sought to prevent France from controlling the Channel coast opposite England. A partition favoring France could have provoked earlier or more sustained Anglo-French rivalry, possibly intensifying naval and colonial competition even before the Seven Years’ War.

Economically, the southern Low Countries were among Europe’s most commercially and industrially dynamic regions. Their early absorption into France might have accelerated French industrial development, especially in textiles and metallurgy. Conversely, the Dutch Republic would have suffered if it lost influence or buffer security there, potentially hastening its 18th-century decline.

Finally, the broader balance of power in Europe would have shifted. The Austrian Netherlands served as a bargaining chip and diplomatic lever in great-power politics. Its partition would have reduced Austria’s influence in Western Europe, pushing Vienna to focus even more on Central and Eastern Europe, possibly intensifying its rivalry with Prussia and the Ottoman Empire.

In sum, a partition of the Austrian Netherlands in the 18th century would likely have strengthened France if it were the main beneficiary, weakened Austria’s western position, altered Anglo-French rivalry, and possibly prevented the later emergence of Belgium as a unified state. The Low Countries might today be politically fragmented rather than forming a distinct Belgian nation.

edus.text: If the Austrian Netherlands (roughly modern Belgium and Luxembourg) had been partitioned in the 18th century, the consequences would have depended on who divided it and when,
but the overall trajectory of Western Europe would likely have shifted in several important ways.
The most plausible moment for partition would have been during the War of the Austrian Succession (1740–1748) or earlier during the War of the Spanish Succession (1701–1714).
France had long sought to push its northeastern frontier to more defensible “natural borders,”
while the Dutch Republic wanted buffer fortresses against French expansion.
Prussia or other German states might also have pressed claims in Luxembourg or Liège.
If Austria had lost control and the territory had been divided primarily between France and the Dutch (or smaller German states),
the strategic buffer between France and the Dutch Republic would have been permanently altered.
If France had annexed most or all of the Austrian Netherlands in the mid-18th century,
it would have gained economically advanced, densely populated, and industrially promising regions decades before the French Revolutionary Wars.
This would have strengthened France financially and militarily before 1789.
The French Revolutionary expansion into Belgium in the 1790s would not have been necessary,
and the ideological export of revolution into the Low Countries might have been more limited or taken a different form.
A pre-revolutionary annexation could also have reduced one of the Revolutionary Wars’ key theaters,
possibly altering coalition dynamics.
If instead the region had been partitioned among smaller powers—say, France taking Flanders, the Dutch taking frontier fortresses, and parts going to German states—
the area might have become fragmented like western Germany.
In that case, no unified Belgian state would likely have emerged in 1830.
The Belgian Revolution depended in part on the territory’s prior administrative unity under Austrian and then French rule.
Without that unity, a coherent Belgian national identity might never have formed,
and the territory might today be divided between France, the Netherlands, and Germany or Luxembourg.
Strategically, an earlier French annexation would have alarmed Britain.
Britain consistently sought to prevent France from controlling the Channel coast opposite England.
A partition favoring France could have provoked earlier or more sustained Anglo-French rivalry,
possibly intensifying naval and colonial competition even before the Seven Years’ War.
Economically, the southern Low Countries were among Europe’s most commercially and industrially dynamic regions.
Their early absorption into France might have accelerated French industrial development, especially in textiles and metallurgy.
Conversely, the Dutch Republic would have suffered if it lost influence or buffer security there,
potentially hastening its 18th-century decline.
Finally, the broader balance of power in Europe would have shifted.
The Austrian Netherlands served as a bargaining chip and diplomatic lever in great-power politics.
Its partition would have reduced Austria’s influence in Western Europe,
pushing Vienna to focus even more on Central and Eastern Europe,
possibly intensifying its rivalry with Prussia and the Ottoman Empire.

In sum, a partition of the Austrian Netherlands in the 18th century would likely have strengthened France if it were the main beneficiary, weakened Austria’s western position, altered Anglo-French rivalry, and possibly prevented the later emergence of Belgium as a unified state.
The Low Countries might today be politically fragmented rather than forming a distinct Belgian nation.

items.question: My Alternative History Scenario: What If Napoleon couldn't make it to France at 1799?
human_answers: It's very obscure and I couldn't track down the reference this morning, which I think came from some book on the First Serbian Uprising. The Turkish fortress on the island blocked easy communication between the Serbs and the Russian forces in Wallachia. Well, Russia sent an auxiliary force into Poland to aid Napoleon, as promised, and was rewarded with Tarnopol in the peace treaty. So it looks like a victory. But in reality as you say Russia did very little but go through the motions and Napoleon gave them the merest scrap of a reward. Despite the common view, I don't think Alexander ingratiated himself to Vienna by doing this and I don't think Austria would have been more active in 1812 had things been different in 1809. Fair enough. Austria was at least thought to be supplying weapons to the Sultan in 1829, though I don't know if that was confirmed to actually be true.

Why would Hapsburgs or Hohenzollerns circa 1803 care about the US? None of them had colonies in the Western hemisphere (or anywhere else) and, IIRC, at that time the former colonies were not ideologically, not to mention economically or militarily, of a any serious importance for the continental Europe. Which, putting aside Spain, leaves “certain trade arrangements” and the obvious question is what these arrangements would be? Would they hurt or benefit France? In OTL to a great degree the French bellicosity was supported by the strategic factor called “Bonaparte” who, besides military glory, provided looting (both on state and individual levels) on the “industrial” scale. It seems that ITTL French government behaves “Napoleonic” without Napoleon, which brings some obvious questions without clear answers to which episode with tearing the document looks as an act of imbecility. AFAIK, none of the OTL generals of that period were that good in both areas and without Bonaparte the war of 2nd coalition most probably would end due to the exhaustion of both sides without too much to show for it (in OTL in 1799 the French were kicked out of Italy and exercises on the Danube led to nowhere for either side so the only area of clear success was Switzerland). Which means that enthusiasm in France is unlikely and, in OTL the Directory was in almost permanent fiscal crisis. So, it would be quite interesting to find out in more details how the things were proceeding (including financial aspect) without Nappy? Were ITTL any indications of the Russian desire to conquer Hungary? Anyway, this was clearly not an consideration during the 2nd Coalition when Austria asked for the Russian help (at least in OTL). BTW, without Nappy, is Paul still on the throne? Alexander hated Napoleon on a personal level, which mostly defined his actions in the 3rd and 4th coalitions, but, while being pro-British, was not actively anti-French in general. Anyway, it does not look like he would be doing Francis’ bidding. Why not Greenland? If Austria is at war with France, whoever is the Russian emperor, can start war with the OE without paying any attention to Vienna’s position. Besides, how would Russia simultaneously fight the French and the OE? Obviously, expecting that after the French war the Hapsburg emperor is going to honor his generous promise to grant Russia the Ottoman territories (how about the Ottoman consent?) assumes a rather unrealistic level of a naivety on the Russian side. Which is of no importance to Vienna and Berlin by the obvious reason: none of them has colonies in the Americas. Then, the US in the early 1800s as a serious military threat? In 1812 it had less than 10,000 troops when war started and its navy had 12 frigates. Yes, and the question is how an obvious idiot managed to become the head of the French government and how his actions got approval of the parliament?
items.original_question: My Alternative History Scenario: What if Napoleon couldn't make it to France at 1799? EPISODE THREE​ German Pact ​ ​ A sudden storm breaking out across Europe had created a massive shockwave. Austria, still struggling to recover from the economic and military wounds of the War of the Second Coalition, was deeply displeased by France’s abrupt rekindling of hostilities. Emperor Francis II had been expecting a long period of peace, one he intended to devote to revitalizing Germany. Unfortunately, history had once again disappointed him. His federalist ambitions had not yet completely faded, but this meant confronting French republicanism earlier than anticipated. Moreover, following the referendum held on 18 February 1803 and the subsequent election, the country transitioned into what was called a presidential system. As a result, Fourier—who came to power and was a prominent representative of socialist thought—began spreading his ideas more widely across Europe. This signified a gradual shift of the German peoples toward republicanism. Although the Kingdom of Prussia and the Habsburg Monarchy did not hold each other in high regard, they shared a common enemy: France and republicanism. Approximately one week had passed since the outbreak of the Franco-Spanish War. French armies advanced rapidly, exploiting the dire condition of the Spanish forces to seize Catalonia and push toward Eastern Aragon. The Basque region had also fallen. Emperor Francis convened his cabinet, and they debated at length what course of action should be taken. Johann Amadeus Franz, the Minister of Finance of the era, was firmly opposed to breaking the peace with France, as any potential war would further devastate Austria’s already fragile economy. József Alvinczi, the Chief of the General Staff, argued that this war represented an opportunity to eliminate both France and the spread of republican ideas on the European continent. He maintained that, as demonstrated in the previous conflict, the Austrian army was not in as poor a condition as believed and demanded that an open ultimatum be issued to France. However, the Emperor had a different plan in mind. Although there was no certainty it would succeed, he deemed it worth attempting. For this reason, he decided to send a delegate to the Kingdom of Prussia, carrying a note requesting a private meeting with the King. The delegation set out on 15 March 1803. Meanwhile, across Europe, no clear decision had yet emerged from the British Isles. Prime Minister Henry Addington had no desire to see Spain under French control, but he also believed that the British Army was not yet prepared. After lengthy discussions with other statesmen, he sent an envoy to the Kingdom of Portugal to further expand the Anglo-Portuguese Alliance and present several proposals. In the meantime, the delegation sent by Austria to Prussia returned two weeks later. The Emperor’s proposal to the King of Prussia was to intervene in the Franco-Spanish War by forming a German coalition. The Prussian King, eager to enhance his prestige among the German states, responded favorably and announced his acceptance. Thus, the German Pact was formed. Both sides began final preparations for their already mobilized armies, and within approximately two weeks, everything was ready. A note bearing the personal signatures of both the Emperor and the King was delivered to the French delegates by a joint Austro-Prussian mission. The note demanded that France sever its alliance with the United States, withdraw from Spain, and agree to certain trade arrangements. French President Charles Fourier tore the original document to pieces in parliament. This act provided the Habsburg Monarchy and the Kingdom of Prussia with sufficient legitimacy to launch a military intervention against France. Emperor Francis II was deeply uneasy about Russia’s ambiguous stance. He neither wanted Russia to emerge excessively strong nor excessively weak. Poland could be the first step, and the Russian flag might one day fly over Hungary or the borders of the Holy Roman Empire. Taking such a risk seemed irrational. Therefore, depending on the course of the war, he considered enticing Russia into joining their side by offering the Balkan territories of the already weakened Ottoman Empire—despite his preference for preserving the balance of power in the Balkans and Eastern Europe. The French threat, however, took precedence. Although the United States did not yet pose a direct threat to Europe, it continued to threaten the colonial powers in the Americas. While it had not yet entered the conflict, such an involvement was not impossible. On the other hand, the Emperor foresaw that the French government’s aggressive and overly idealistic actions would ultimately lead to its downfall. By initiating this war, France had effectively shot itself in the foot, and these events would pave the way for a rise in anti-French sentiment throughout Europe.

criteria.name: Counterfactual Premise Fidelity (Napoleon Absent from 1799 Coup)
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the response consistently respects the core premise that Napoleon fails to return to France in 1799 and therefore cannot lead the Coup of 18 Brumaire or personally shape subsequent French policy.
criteria.1-2: Ignores or reverses the premise (e.g., Napoleon still seizes power in 1799) or treats his absence as trivial.
criteria.3-4: Mentions his absence but allows him indirect control or reintroduces him without explanation.
criteria.5-6: Keeps him absent from power but leaves unclear who replaces him or how the coup crisis resolves.
criteria.7-8: Clearly replaces Napoleon with plausible alternative actors (e.g., Directory survival, another general, royalist shift) and maintains premise consistency.
criteria.9-10: Rigorously maintains his absence across all developments and systematically explores how the lack of his leadership alters French domestic and foreign trajectories.

criteria.name: Causal Mechanism Depth (France and the Second Coalition)
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates the specificity and plausibility of mechanisms explaining how France, the Directory, and the Second Coalition evolve without Napoleon’s return.
criteria.1-2: Relies on vague claims (e.g., “France collapses” or “Coalition wins”) with no mechanisms.
criteria.3-4: Provides limited or generic mechanisms without linking them to 1799 military or political realities.
criteria.5-6: Identifies some relevant mechanisms (military exhaustion, fiscal crisis, rival generals) but with limited detail.
criteria.7-8: Explains concrete pathways (e.g., alternative generals’ performance, fiscal instability, coalition diplomacy, British naval dominance).
criteria.9-10: Offers a historically grounded, multi-factor causal chain integrating military performance, domestic politics, coalition cohesion, and leadership dynamics.

criteria.name: Long-Range European System Effects (1800–1815 and Beyond)
criteria.criteria_description: Measures how well the answer traces medium- and long-term ripple effects across Europe (Austria, Russia, Britain, Prussia, Ottoman Empire) in the absence of Napoleonic rule.
criteria.1-2: Stops at immediate 1799–1800 effects with no broader implications.
criteria.3-4: Mentions later events (e.g., no Napoleonic Wars) but without structured projection.
criteria.5-6: Projects several downstream effects but with limited interconnection or timeframe clarity.
criteria.7-8: Coherently tracks systemic consequences (balance of power, Holy Roman Empire, Russian policy, British strategy) over multiple years.
criteria.9-10: Develops an integrated long-range scenario showing how altered French leadership reshapes coalition patterns, territorial settlements, and the European balance of power.

criteria.name: Internal Coherence and Contradiction Control
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses logical consistency across the scenario, including alignment between military outcomes, political structures, and diplomatic behavior.
criteria.1-2: Contains major contradictions (e.g., weakened France simultaneously dominating Europe without explanation).
criteria.3-4: Minor contradictions or unexplained leaps in political or military capacity.
criteria.5-6: Generally coherent but with some strained assumptions or under-justified shifts.
criteria.7-8: Logically consistent with only minor speculative gaps, and assumptions are mostly aligned with capabilities.
criteria.9-10: Fully coherent scenario where military, fiscal, diplomatic, and ideological elements mutually reinforce each other without contradiction.

criteria.name: Uncertainty Calibration and Plausibility Framing
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer appropriately distinguishes between high-confidence historical constraints and speculative extensions in this alternative 1799 scenario.
criteria.1-2: Presents speculation as certainty or ignores historical constraints.
criteria.3-4: Acknowledges uncertainty superficially but overstates conclusions.
criteria.5-6: Recognizes key uncertainties (e.g., coalition cohesion, French domestic politics) but unevenly.
criteria.7-8: Clearly signals contingency points and compares multiple plausible pathways.
criteria.9-10: Carefully weighs alternative branches, explicitly discusses probability ranges, and grounds speculation in known structural constraints of 1799–early 19th-century Europe.

items.model_answer:
If Napoleon had been unable to return to France in 1799—whether captured by the British, killed in Egypt, or politically stranded—the Coup of 18 Brumaire would almost certainly not have occurred in the form we know it. The Directory was already unstable, unpopular, and widely seen as corrupt and ineffective. However, without Napoleon’s prestige, military reputation, and political ambition, the specific consolidation of power that produced the Consulate and later the Empire would likely not have happened.

In the short term, France would probably have remained under the Directory a while longer, but it was structurally weak. Another general—perhaps Jourdan, Moreau, or even Bernadotte—might have emerged as a political figure. Of these, Moreau is the most plausible candidate for a stabilizing military strongman, though he lacked Napoleon’s ruthlessness and political instinct. A coup was still likely, but it might have produced a more collective military regime rather than a single dominant ruler.

Without Napoleon’s centralized authority, France’s military campaigns would have been more cautious. The Second Coalition might have pushed France back to its “natural borders,” especially if French command remained divided. It is unlikely that France would have achieved the sweeping victories at Marengo (1800) and Austerlitz (1805) in the same decisive way. As a result, Austria and possibly Britain would have retained stronger positions on the continent.

Most significantly, Europe would have avoided the Napoleonic Empire and the series of massive wars from 1803 to 1815 that reshaped the continent. There would likely have been no Confederation of the Rhine, no dissolution of the Holy Roman Empire in 1806 (at least not then), and no Peninsular War in its historical form. Prussia and Austria might have remained dominant in German affairs without the shock of Napoleonic defeat forcing reforms.

Domestically, however, many revolutionary reforms would probably have endured. The abolition of feudalism, secularization, and legal equality were already embedded in French society. But the Napoleonic Code, the Concordat with the Church in its specific form, and the highly centralized administrative state might have developed more gradually or differently.

In the long run, nationalism in Germany, Italy, and Spain might have risen more slowly. The chain reaction that eventually contributed to the revolutions of 1848 and even to German unification in 1871 would have been delayed or reshaped. Britain would still have been France’s main rival, but without a continent-spanning Napoleonic threat, British global expansion might have proceeded with less urgency.

In short, without Napoleon’s return in 1799, France likely would still have experienced authoritarian consolidation, but not the sweeping imperial project that transformed Europe. The map of Europe would have changed more gradually, and the intense cycle of coalition warfare from 1803 to 1815 would probably never have reached the same scale or decisiveness.

As a result, Austria and possibly Britain would have retained stronger positions on the continent.
Most significantly, Europe would have avoided the Napoleonic Empire and the series of massive wars from 1803 to 1815 that reshaped the continent.
There would likely have been no Confederation of the Rhine, no dissolution of the Holy Roman Empire in 1806 (at least not then), and no Peninsular War in its historical form.
Prussia and Austria might have remained dominant in German affairs without the shock of Napoleonic defeat forcing reforms.
Domestically, however, many revolutionary reforms would probably have endured.
The abolition of feudalism, secularization, and legal equality were already embedded in French society.
But the Napoleonic Code, the Concordat with the Church in its specific form, and the highly centralized administrative state might have developed more gradually or differently.
In the long run, nationalism in Germany, Italy, and Spain might have risen more slowly.
The chain reaction that eventually contributed to the revolutions of 1848 and even to German unification in 1871 would have been delayed or reshaped.
Britain would still have been France’s main rival,
but without a continent-spanning Napoleonic threat, British global expansion might have proceeded with less urgency.
In short, without Napoleon’s return in 1799, France likely would still have experienced authoritarian consolidation, but not the sweeping imperial project that transformed Europe.
The map of Europe would have changed more gradually, and the intense cycle of coalition warfare from 1803 to 1815 would probably never have reached the same scale or decisiveness.

items.question: What If the Greek 'Great Plan' had succeeded and the Greek War of Independence had triggered an early collapse of the Ottoman Empire?
human_answers: A more decisive Ottoman defeat against Greece can give birth to the "Megali Idea" before 1844. In such a scenario, a larger independent Greek state can invited Louis-Philippe d’Orléans to become its king, before 1830 of course. This arrangement can be supported by both France and its Bourbon king, who might want to sideline a troublesome cousin, and by the United Kingdom. For the British, the presence of a Great European power south of the Straits, one aligned with neither Austria nor Russia can further divide the continental great powers and serve British strategic interests. With France satisfied in Greece and Austria compensated with territories along the Adriatic coast, Britain can focus on securing Egypt for itself. Even if the Suez Canal is not even a dream, control of Egypt is already strategically valuable for strengthening connections with India. By 1829, railway projects are already under consideration, making overland transit increasingly plausible and reinforcing Egypt’s geopolitical importance. And if its happen after 1830, Louis-Philippe has enough sons (6 minus one who died in 1828) to send one to Greece.

Considering their interest is not even religious (GB: Protestant, France: Catholic, Russia: Orthodox) and that really none of these Great Powers saw the Greek War of Independence with positive eyes (to them it was no different than the revolutions in Spain, Portugal and Naples; which, btw, they sent huge armies to crush). There was later a British change, but even the Metternich, Alexander and so on weren't super happy about it. Remember: at this point, the memory of Napoleon is far fresher than that of the Ottoman invasions into the Balkans, so the concern, far above Islam, is revolutionary sentiment. What I do see happening is them deliberating and taking too long to make a decision that the situation ends up devolving on its own (it took them like 3 years to agree to send an invasion to Spain). Then again, the French were sympathetic to Muhammad Ali while the British aided Ali Pasha plenty of times (through Maitland, specifically). They will always prefer a rotting corpse of the Ottoman empire maintaining power over the ambitious and reformist Albanian Pashas in power, this is why they went out of their way to put them out IRL, but when shit hits the fan, they have to re-examine their approach of course.

Agreed that the Great Powers, including even Russia under Alexander, don't want a full Ottoman collapse. That's not the same as saying they would intervene to stop it. It's hard to conceive of a situation in which Great Britain, France, or Russia would go to war to suppress Christian rebels fighting against the Sultan, particularly after the various atrocities committed at Chios and other places. There were also similar atrocities committed by the Greeks against Muslims, but this did not register in the European consciousness of the time and would not be a factor. It's also not a given that any intervention would be successful at stopping chaos and preserving the Empire, even if it did somehow occur. This would be a formidable job if the situation became so extreme that the Ottomans asked for such support. More likely the intervention would be directed towards managing the collapse and achieving a partition either formally or in terms of spheres of influence.
items.original_question: What if 'Great Plan' more or fully successful - Greek War of Independence causes early Ottoman collapse? There have been many threads about the Greek War of Independence here, but one what if I haven't seen anyone talk about might be one of the most crazy ones. Mark Mazower states the following in his book on the Greek War of Indepdendence: Of course, aside from the revolt in the Peloponnese, none of these plans ever came close to succeeding. These plans were modified or abandoned entirely when the focus of the revolt shifted from the Peloponnese to the Danubian Principalities. There was a letter sent to cause terror in Constantinople, but the letter never made it and plans were changing so often that no action was taken. Now this seems like an insane scheme which would be insanely hard to pull off, even if all the circumstances were right, but let's hypothetically ask, what if some, or all of them did? Would this cause the Ottoman Empire to collapse entirely, or enter a prolonged period of unrest? A torching of the fleet, coordinated with the assassination of Mahmud II, coupled with all the other issues the empire was facing in the early 1820's seem like they would be a complete headache, who would even be Sultan had this happened, considering Abdulmecid wasn't even born yet and Mahmud II had no sons? Edit: Turns out Mahmud II had a single surviving son by this point, Abdulhamid. But he died in 1825 IOTL, which, if it still happens, might actually make things even worse if the revolt didn't fizzle out by then.

If the Greek “Great Plan” (Megali Idea) had effectively succeeded during the Greek War of Independence (1821–1829) and triggered an early collapse of the Ottoman Empire, the political map of southeastern Europe and the eastern Mediterranean would have changed dramatically decades before it did historically.

First, Greece would likely have emerged not as a small kingdom centered on the Peloponnese and central Greece, but as a much larger state incorporating Constantinople, western Anatolia’s Aegean coast, and possibly much of Thrace and Macedonia. Such a state would have claimed continuity with Byzantium, positioning itself as the restored heir of the Eastern Roman Empire. Constantinople—rather than Athens—might have become the capital, making Greece a major imperial power rather than a small nationalist state.

An early Ottoman collapse in the 1820s or 1830s would also have radically reshaped Balkan nationalism. Historically, Serbia, Bulgaria, Romania, and others gained autonomy or independence gradually over the 19th century as Ottoman authority weakened. If the empire had fragmented abruptly, multiple national revolutions might have erupted simultaneously. The result could have been either a patchwork of small nation-states formed earlier—or violent competition over mixed territories like Macedonia and Thrace even sooner than occurred historically. Ethnic cleansing and population displacement, which marked the Balkan Wars and early 20th century, might have begun nearly a century earlier.

Great Power politics would have been transformed. Russia, Britain, and France intervened in Greek independence partly to manage Ottoman decline. A sudden Ottoman collapse would have intensified rivalry over the “Eastern Question.” Russia might have pushed aggressively toward the Straits, claiming to protect Orthodox Christians. Britain would likely have tried to prevent Russian control of Constantinople to safeguard Mediterranean and Indian trade routes. Austria would have feared nationalist contagion among its own Slavic populations. A large Greek state controlling the Straits might have become either a British client to counter Russia or a battleground for influence. The Crimean War, instead of occurring in the 1850s, might have come decades earlier—or taken a different form entirely.

In the Middle East, the absence of Ottoman authority in the 1830s would have created a power vacuum. Egypt under Muhammad Ali was already semi-autonomous and expansionist; it might have carved out an independent empire across Syria and Arabia. European colonial penetration of the Levant and Mesopotamia could have accelerated, potentially leading to earlier French and British protectorates. Without a late-19th-century Ottoman reform era (Tanzimat), modernization efforts in the region would have been more fragmented and externally driven.

Internally, a “Greater Greece” would have faced immense challenges. Large Muslim populations in Anatolia and Thrace would have complicated governance. The state might have struggled with financial insolvency and administrative overstretch, much as it did historically even on a smaller scale. Intercommunal tensions could have produced earlier cycles of violence between Christians and Muslims, possibly foreshadowing something like the Greco-Turkish population exchange nearly a century earlier.

Finally, the long-term trajectory toward World War I might have shifted significantly. An early Ottoman collapse would remove one of the key declining empires whose weakness destabilized Europe. But it might also have intensified Austro-Russian rivalry in the Balkans sooner. If Austria or Russia had clashed earlier over former Ottoman lands, a major European war could have erupted in the mid-19th century instead of 1914—or the balance of power might have stabilized differently, preventing the specific chain of events that led to World War I.

In short, a successful Great Plan and early Ottoman collapse would likely have produced a larger, more ambitious Greek state, accelerated Balkan nationalism, intensified Great Power rivalry over the eastern Mediterranean, and reshaped both European and Middle Eastern political development—potentially moving many of the region’s 20th-century conflicts into the 19th century.

edus.text: If the Greek “Great Plan” (Megali Idea) had effectively succeeded during the Greek War of Independence (1821–1829) and triggered an early collapse of the Ottoman Empire,
the political map of southeastern Europe and the eastern Mediterranean would have changed dramatically decades before it did historically.
First, Greece would likely have emerged not as a small kingdom centered on the Peloponnese and central Greece,
but as a much larger state incorporating Constantinople, western Anatolia’s Aegean coast, and possibly much of Thrace and Macedonia.
Such a state would have claimed continuity with Byzantium,
positioning itself as the restored heir of the Eastern Roman Empire.
Constantinople—rather than Athens—might have become the capital,
making Greece a major imperial power rather than a small nationalist state.
An early Ottoman collapse in the 1820s or 1830s would also have radically reshaped Balkan nationalism.
Historically, Serbia, Bulgaria, Romania, and others gained autonomy or independence gradually over the 19th century as Ottoman authority weakened.
If the empire had fragmented abruptly,
multiple national revolutions might have erupted simultaneously.
The result could have been either a patchwork of small nation-states formed earlier
or violent competition over mixed territories like Macedonia and Thrace even sooner than occurred historically.
Ethnic cleansing and population displacement, which marked the Balkan Wars and early 20th century, might have begun nearly a century earlier.
Great Power politics would have been transformed.
Russia, Britain, and France intervened in Greek independence partly to manage Ottoman decline.
A sudden Ottoman collapse would have intensified rivalry over the “Eastern Question.”
Russia might have pushed aggressively toward the Straits, claiming to protect Orthodox Christians.
Britain would likely have tried to prevent Russian control of Constantinople to safeguard Mediterranean and Indian trade routes.
Austria would have feared nationalist contagion among its own Slavic populations.
A large Greek state controlling the Straits might have become either a British client to counter Russia or a battleground for influence.
The Crimean War might have come decades earlier or taken a different form entirely.
In the Middle East, the absence of Ottoman authority in the 1830s would have created a power vacuum.
Egypt under Muhammad Ali was already semi-autonomous and expansionist;
it might have carved out an independent empire across Syria and Arabia.
European colonial penetration of the Levant and Mesopotamia could have accelerated,
potentially leading to earlier French and British protectorates.
Without a late-19th-century Ottoman reform era (Tanzimat),
modernization efforts in the region would have been more fragmented and externally driven.
Internally, a “Greater Greece” would have faced immense challenges.
Large Muslim populations in Anatolia and Thrace would have complicated governance.
The state might have struggled with financial insolvency and administrative overstretch,
much as it did historically even on a smaller scale.
Intercommunal tensions could have produced earlier cycles of violence between Christians and Muslims,
possibly foreshadowing something like the Greco-Turkish population exchange nearly a century earlier.
Finally, the long-term trajectory toward World War I might have shifted significantly.
An early Ottoman collapse would remove one of the key declining empires whose weakness destabilized Europe.
But it might also have intensified Austro-Russian rivalry in the Balkans sooner.
If Austria or Russia had clashed earlier over former Ottoman lands,
a major European war could have erupted in the mid-19th century instead of 1914
or the balance of power might have stabilized differently, preventing the specific chain of events that led to World War I.

In short, a successful Great Plan and early Ottoman collapse would likely have produced a larger, more ambitious Greek state, accelerated Balkan nationalism, intensified Great Power rivalry over the eastern Mediterranean, and reshaped both European and Middle Eastern political development,
potentially moving many of the region’s 20th-century conflicts into the 19th century.

items.question: What If the French become one of the largest communities in the US
human_answers: Hordes of Catholics, even if not all that devout, descending on the US will cause some tension. On the flip side, though, France is one of the civilized nations, and they're seen as more desirable shade of white. Timing matters, too. Napoleonic era, when immigration is still low, is a whole lot different than the final decades of the 19th century, when millions is a drop in the bucket. Location matters, too. Are the French hordes joining into the crowded East, where they likely assimilate? Or are they carving out a big chunk of the midwest/west as largely French? Reason for the diaspora might matter. If we mess with the Napoleonic era, especially if we butterfly it (not killing off a generation or two of males would be a good start in having excess population to export), the state of the world could affect the state of the USA (maybe even the size if no Mex-Am War/Texas). With such a generic What if, we can only talk in generics. If we stipulate a recognizable world, more or less the same, except a massive French diaspora for some reason that hasn't caused OTL to derail.... I would guess the French would be like any other large group. There'll be tension, but everyone will adapt. It's an age of racism, and French are in the top class, so I suspect they'll have an easier time of it. (caveat edit: In no way am I saying French are better than any other nation, but reality is that skin color mattered. My understanding is that not all whites were considered equal)

I would assume rather than staying in the east, the French would largely settle in former Louisiana- centring probably on New Orleans. Texas and Florida as well are likely spots for French settlement. Of the 13 colonies, I would guess it’s the southern ones which would be most amenable to French settlement- though how that affects racial dynamics in the south, and how that affects potential north south tensions is difficult to say. It’s difficult as well to say what the economic impact of French settlement would be- I’d say as a community they’d probably be more educated and thus better off than the Irish or Italians, perhaps more comparable to German or Swedish immigrants. Perhaps the planter class ends up going fully bilingual. Depending on how the 19th century goes you could end up with an Alt-confederacy that stays independent because it has so many French speakers and Catholics that the north simply isn’t interested in reintegrating them.
items.original_question: What if the French become one of the largest communities in the US Let’s suppose that millions of French flocked to the US in the 19th century for one reason or another—for example, because harsher Napoleonic Wars and a more severe Congress of Vienna plunged France into a deep economic crisis, while the Irish and Italians would be less numerous in the US, for example because the Irish Great Famine never happened and the Italian peninsula unified and modernized earlier. No PoD before 1780. How would the French be treated in the US? Would they face xenophobia and form a distinct community like the Irish and Italians, or would they be assimilated among the WASPs within one or two generations like the Germans did IOTL? French culture was admired, but I’m not sure that the arrival of millions of French people (with a Latin culture and Catholic religion) would be particularly well received.

items.model_answer:
If the French became one of the largest communities in the United States—comparable in size and influence to English, German, or Spanish-speaking populations—the country’s cultural, political, and linguistic landscape would look noticeably different.

First, language would likely be more multilingual at a national level. French might hold a semi-official or widely recognized status alongside English, especially in regions with dense French settlement. Public signage, education, and government services could commonly appear in both English and French. States beyond Louisiana—perhaps in the Midwest, Northeast, or along major migration corridors—might have strong francophone identities. American English itself would probably absorb more French vocabulary and pronunciation patterns than it already has.

Second, religion and social traditions might shift. Historically, many French immigrants were Catholic, so a large French population could strengthen Catholic institutions, schools, and political influence, particularly in earlier centuries. Holidays, festivals, and cuisine—such as regional French food traditions—would be more deeply embedded in mainstream American culture, not just seen as elite or “foreign.” National tastes in food, fashion, and art might lean more heavily toward French styles, potentially reshaping everything from architecture in major cities to culinary norms in everyday households.

Politically, foreign policy might tilt differently. A stronger French-American bloc could influence U.S. relations with France, Canada (especially Quebec), and parts of Africa and the Caribbean. The U.S. might engage more deeply with francophone countries and institutions. Domestically, debates over federalism, secularism, and education could reflect French intellectual traditions, particularly ideas about centralized administration and laïcité (strict secularism in public life).

Regionally, areas like Louisiana might not stand out as unique enclaves but instead be part of a broader francophone cultural belt. If French settlement had expanded westward more robustly (as it did during the colonial era), the cultural imprint across the Mississippi Valley might be stronger today, possibly influencing place names, legal traditions, and land-use patterns more deeply than they already do.

Overall, the United States would likely remain recognizably American—shaped by constitutional principles and waves of diverse immigration—but it would feel more linguistically bilingual, culturally tied to French traditions, and perhaps more closely connected to the francophone world in its identity and global outlook.

He would have zero troubles in giving back the half of her dowry he had already received (for all that getting back her dowry meant that Catherine had no right to any English money or lands) and send Catherine back at home as he had no use for her. Catalina’s aunt, the Dowager Queen of Naples would first try to marry her own daughter to the new Ferdinand III of Naples, as Giovanna was still in her mid-20s (or she would expect to see another match arranged for her daughter before agreeing to support Catalina as future Queen of Naples. Sea journeys at the time were extremely dangerous (I don’t remember if Catalina got lucky, but both Joanna and Margaret got close to die in their respective wedding journeys) reason for which Philip used his friendship with the French King for securing a land passage into France for going to receive the investitures. Eleanor and Charles at the time were too little for making safely the long journey, for not talking about baby Isabella, and Philip would never agree to bring them in Castile in any case. And if she had been so inclined Catalina, being the youngest of her sisters, could very well be allowed to take the veil. In 1502 Juana had three children and Maria one and both were likely to have soon more…

The year 1502 starts very rough for Catalina of Aragon. She and her husband, Arthur , Prince of Wales had both fallen ill at the end of March and when she recovered, she discovered that her husband had died. She could not believe it. She was a widow after only five months of marriage. She knew that she was not pregnant, as her marriage was unconsummated. One month after she was made a widow, Catalina was moved to Durham House in London and was visited by King Henry VII and his wife, Queen Elizabeth of York. Catalina told them that she had bled already and there was no hope for an heir from their late son, so his younger brother, Prince Henry, Duke of York, was officially declared as the heir. When the news to Catalina's parents, King Fernando II of Aragon and Queen Isabella I of Castile, they were disappointed that the alliance seemed to have fallen through and that their daughter was widowed at only sixteen years old. This began a struggle over Catalina. Queen Isabella was adamant that her youngest child be returned to her, since there was not a hope of an English grandchild to seal the alliance with Spain and England. King Henry VII, however, did not want to lose her or her dowry. He offered to marry her to his younger son and she could still be Queen of England one day. Queen Isabella made up her mind and told her husband that she wanted their daughter to be returned home. King Ferdinand sent an ambassador to tell King Henry that the Princess would be returned to Spain, either with her entourage or by force. When King Henry VII heard this, he was furious, but also terrified. He needed this alliance with Spain and he did not want to let his daughter-in-law go. Finally, an agreement was finally reached. The Infanta would return to her parents and half her dowry would be returned with her and she would retain her status of Dowager Princess of Wales and would still receive her marriage jointure for the remainder of her life. Her English attendants, like Margaret Pole, would remain in England. When she was told Princess Catalina had a mix of grief and relief. She was happy to return home to her parents, especially since her older sister, Juana, who was now Princess of Asturias, was back home as well. On August 1, 1502, Princess Catalina and her entourage arrived at Dover, preparing to board the ship that will cross the sea once again. Prince Henry, the young Prince of Wales accompanied her, just like he escorted her down the aisle to marry his late older brother. The eleven year old, who was talkative and social, was unusually quiet through the journey. Princess Catalina gave him a little kiss on his forehead and told him that she will never forget him or her time in England and she knew that one day, he will be the greatest King that England ever had, before she boarded the ship. Thankfully, this journey was much easier than her original one taking her to England. She and her entourage arrived in Laredo on the 15th of August. Princess Catalina found herself smiling, as she saw the familiar Castilian villages and knew she was home. However, she then was wondering what would happen to her and her future. Due to the deaths of her older brother, sister and nephew, she knew that taking holy vows was not an option, as he parents only had three surviving daughters. Would she just remain a spinster? Would she be married off again to a foreign Kingdom, even France? Her father was definitely ambitious and was a shrewd ruler, so she knew that she would not remain unmarried for long, but she was still looking forward to just feeling her mother's embrace once more.

items.model_answer:
If Catherine of Aragon had married Ferdinand, Duke of Calabria, in 1505 instead of becoming Henry VIII’s queen, the political and religious trajectory of England—and to a lesser extent Italy and Spain—would likely have changed profoundly.

In 1505 Catherine was still technically the widow of Arthur, Prince of Wales, and her future in England was uncertain. A marriage to Ferdinand, Duke of Calabria (the heir to the dispossessed Neapolitan royal house of Aragon), would have kept her firmly within the orbit of Spanish dynastic politics rather than English ones. This would have strengthened Aragonese claims in southern Italy and possibly reinforced Spanish influence in Naples during the ongoing Italian Wars. Catherine, daughter of Ferdinand and Isabella, would have been a prestigious match, bolstering the duke’s legitimacy and perhaps positioning Naples more securely within the Spanish imperial system rather than as a contested territory between France and Spain.

For England, the consequences would have been dramatic. Henry VIII would not have married Catherine in 1509. Without that marriage, there would have been no prolonged struggle over the lack of a surviving male heir, and thus no “Great Matter”—Henry’s campaign to annul his marriage on the grounds of biblical prohibition. The English Reformation, at least in its initial form, was driven by Henry’s desire to remarry and secure a male successor. If Catherine had never been his wife, there would have been no need to seek a papal annulment and no immediate trigger for the break with Rome in the 1530s.

This does not mean England would have remained permanently Catholic. Protestant ideas were already spreading in Europe, and reformist currents existed within England. However, without royal sponsorship, reform would likely have proceeded more slowly and perhaps along lines similar to those in Spain or Italy—internal Catholic reform rather than schism. The Church of England as a separate national church might never have emerged, or it might have arisen later under different circumstances.

Dynastically, Henry would have needed another bride. He might have married into the French royal family, a German princely house, or another Iberian line. A French marriage, for instance, could have shifted England’s alliances during the Italian Wars, potentially aligning England more closely with France against the Habsburgs. Alternatively, a Habsburg match could have tied England more tightly to the emerging empire of Charles V. The specific choice would have significantly shaped European power politics in the early sixteenth century.

Mary I of England would never have been born, eliminating the later Marian restoration of Catholicism. Likewise, Elizabeth I—daughter of Anne Boleyn—would not have existed in her historical form, since Anne’s rise depended on Henry’s desire to replace Catherine. Without Elizabeth, England’s later religious settlement, naval expansion, and cultural “Elizabethan” flowering would have taken a different shape, perhaps under a Tudor son by another queen or under a different dynasty if the succession faltered.

In Naples, Catherine as duchess (and potentially queen, depending on how events unfolded) would have brought formidable political skill and dynastic prestige. She was well educated, devout, and experienced in governance. Her presence might have strengthened Aragonese-Spanish authority in southern Italy, but Naples’ fate would still largely depend on the broader Habsburg-Valois struggle. Given Spain’s eventual dominance in Italy under Charles V, Catherine’s marriage could have symbolized and reinforced that consolidation.

In sum, Catherine marrying Ferdinand of Calabria in 1505 would likely have prevented the immediate cause of England’s break with Rome, reshaped Tudor succession, and altered the diplomatic alignments of early sixteenth-century Europe. The English Reformation as we know it—rooted in Henry VIII’s marital crisis—might never have occurred, or would have emerged later and in a very different form.

items.question: What If Dynamite Invented During the Renaissance?
human_answers: I was also wondering how this would affect Venice’s canals but I just realized they’re currently going through the Italian Wars… my idea is 1450: Some guy in London blows himself up mixing soap with aqua fortis and oil of vitriol. Thomas Norton records this in his books on alchemy and knowledge of “aqua ignis” is published. 1470: The War of Roses reaches its peak, Tudors and Lancastrians flee to France and while Yorkists flee to Flanders. These exiled nobles hire alchemists find ways using "aqua ignis” in warfare but their resources are too few and the substance is too difficult to be produced. The formula becomes widespread across the continent and beyond. 1490: King Charles VIII of France commissions “flasks of aqua ignis” to be used in his invasion of Italy alongside the newly invented arquebus. Aqua ignis however is incredibly unstable and soldiers are unable to transport the substance without blowing themselves up. The French effort is widely considered a failure, but his ideas are noted by the Venetians as they go to war with the Pope. 1500: Alchemists in Venice (maybe a little da Vinci cameo but he was hardly an alchemist) start experimenting on ignium and make some interesting observations. They discover that “aqua ignis” stabilizes when mixed with wood pulp and chalk, creating the formula for dynamite which becomes known as “ignium”. However, alchemists fail to produce enough oil of vitriol to make mass produced ignuim viable in warfare. 1540: Paracelcus, the Swiss German alchemist, discovers Joshua Ward’s method for creating sulfuric acid around 200 years early. When mixing sulfur and saltpeter inside giant glass wars with a bit of water, the vapor condenses into oil of vitriol. He dies soon after from mercury poisoning, but the Holy Roman Emperor makes note of his discovery. 1550: The last of the Italian Wars begin. Swiss pike squares, French gunmen, and Ottoman raiders are blown to bits by barrels of ignium catapulted across the battlefield. The Hapsburgs eagerly adopt this new weapon, setting up new factories to mass produce ignium in Germany and Iberia. Meanwhile, alchemists and dissenting thinkers fleeing the counter reformation bring these methods of production to the Emperor’s enemies. Christendom is split in two, a new world is discovered, and the face of warfare is changed forever by this new invention.
items.original_question: What if Dynamite Invented During the Renaissance? Dynamite in our world was invented in 1867 by Alfred Noble as a way to stabilize nitroglycerin, an explosive mix of nitric and sulfuric acids with glycerol (the main ingredient in fat-based soap), by mixing it with clay and chalk. Nitroglycerin, however was only discovered 20 years before Noble’s invention earned him the Noble Prize. But what if things were different? Aqua fortis (nitric acid) and oil of vitriol (sulfuric acid) both existed in medieval Europe and were used by OTL alchemists to dissolve gold for their experiments. Maybe an alchemist tries perfecting the ingredient to turn lead into gold but spills his formula all over his workbench. And when he tries to clean up it up with a soapy rag, he blows himself up, leaving his apprentice to record this newfound discovery. In any case, the year is 1450 and King Henry VI’s “alchemy craze” has taken England by storm. In this craze, nitroglycerin is discovered. Maybe it takes several more decades, if not a century, before alchemists learn how to turn this strange concoction into dynamite. What next?

If dynamite had been invented during the Renaissance—say in the 15th or 16th century—it would likely have accelerated several major transformations already underway in Europe and beyond.

Militarily, the Renaissance was an era of rapid change driven by gunpowder weapons, cannons, and fortified cities designed to withstand artillery. Dynamite, being far more powerful and portable than black powder, would have dramatically increased the destructive capability of armies and navies. Siege warfare would have shifted quickly: fortified walls, even the advanced star forts designed to resist cannon fire, might have become obsolete much sooner. This could have centralized power faster in emerging nation-states, since rulers with access to dynamite could crush rebellious cities and rival nobles more decisively. At the same time, the scale of battlefield destruction would likely have intensified, potentially making wars shorter but more devastating.

In exploration and empire-building, dynamite would have made mining and infrastructure projects far easier. Renaissance Europe was entering the age of global exploration and colonial expansion. Easier excavation of minerals—especially silver and gold in the Americas—could have accelerated the flow of wealth into Europe, strengthening imperial powers like Spain and Portugal earlier and more dramatically. Road-building, canal construction, and harbor development would also have advanced more quickly, possibly speeding up economic integration and trade networks.

Architecturally and scientifically, the Renaissance was marked by ambitious engineering projects—cathedrals, domes, canals, and early scientific experimentation. Dynamite could have enabled more daring construction, tunneling, and quarrying, potentially advancing civil engineering by centuries. However, the scientific understanding of chemistry at the time was limited. Without modern safety protocols and materials science, dynamite production would likely have been unstable and extremely dangerous. Accidental explosions in dense urban centers could have been frequent and catastrophic.

Politically and socially, access to such a powerful explosive might have destabilized societies. Renaissance Europe was already rife with religious conflict and peasant uprisings. Dynamite in the hands of rebels, mercenaries, or assassins could have amplified political violence. The Reformation and subsequent religious wars might have become even more destructive, possibly leading to harsher state surveillance and control earlier in history.

Globally, if European powers possessed dynamite during early encounters with the Americas, Africa, and Asia, the imbalance of military power could have been even more extreme. Conquests might have occurred faster and with greater devastation, reshaping demographic and cultural histories even more dramatically.

Overall, dynamite in the Renaissance would likely have accelerated state centralization, imperial expansion, military transformation, and large-scale engineering—while also increasing the destructiveness of war and political conflict. It would not have changed the direction of history entirely, but it could have compressed centuries of technological and political development into a much shorter, more violent span.

edus.text: If dynamite had been invented during the Renaissance—say in the 15th or 16th century—it would likely have accelerated several major transformations already underway in Europe and beyond.
Militarily, the Renaissance was an era of rapid change driven by gunpowder weapons, cannons, and fortified cities designed to withstand artillery.
Dynamite, being far more powerful and portable than black powder, would have dramatically increased the destructive capability of armies and navies.
Siege warfare would have shifted quickly: fortified walls, even the advanced star forts designed to resist cannon fire, might have become obsolete much sooner.
This could have centralized power faster in emerging nation-states, since rulers with access to dynamite could crush rebellious cities and rival nobles more decisively.
At the same time, the scale of battlefield destruction would likely have intensified, potentially making wars shorter but more devastating.
In exploration and empire-building, dynamite would have made mining and infrastructure projects far easier.
Renaissance Europe was entering the age of global exploration and colonial expansion.

Easier excavation of minerals—especially silver and gold in the Americas—could have accelerated the flow of wealth into Europe, strengthening imperial powers like Spain and Portugal earlier and more dramatically.
Road-building, canal construction, and harbor development would also have advanced more quickly, possibly speeding up economic integration and trade networks.
Architecturally and scientifically, the Renaissance was marked by ambitious engineering projects—cathedrals, domes, canals, and early scientific experimentation.
Dynamite could have enabled more daring construction, tunneling, and quarrying, potentially advancing civil engineering by centuries.
However, the scientific understanding of chemistry at the time was limited.
Without modern safety protocols and materials science, dynamite production would likely have been unstable and extremely dangerous.
Accidental explosions in dense urban centers could have been frequent and catastrophic.
Politically and socially, access to such a powerful explosive might have destabilized societies.
Renaissance Europe was already rife with religious conflict and peasant uprisings.
Dynamite in the hands of rebels, mercenaries, or assassins could have amplified political violence.
The Reformation and subsequent religious wars might have become even more destructive, possibly leading to harsher state surveillance and control earlier in history.
Globally, if European powers possessed dynamite during early encounters with the Americas, Africa, and Asia, the imbalance of military power could have been even more extreme.
Conquests might have occurred faster and with greater devastation, reshaping demographic and cultural histories even more dramatically.

Overall, dynamite in the Renaissance would likely have accelerated state centralization, imperial expansion, military transformation, and large-scale engineering—while also increasing the destructiveness of war and political conflict.
It would not have changed the direction of history entirely, but it could have compressed centuries of technological and political development into a much shorter, more violent span.

items.original_question: What if No Seven Bishops' Death in 1558? Everyone knows about the death of Cardinal Pole, Archbishop of Canterbury shortly after Queen Mary in 1558. But less known- as in, not even listed when you google them- is that there were six other bishops who died around the same time (including Maurice Griffith, Bishop of Rochester). This led to the opening of several vacancies in the English Catholic Church at the start of Elizabeth I's reign. To the seven bishops who died, can be added Bishop Oglethorpe of Carlisle (who, while he crowned Elizabeth, was no fan of hers after she stormed out of his celebration of Christmas Mass in 1558 because he defied her) and Nicolas Heath, the archbishop of York, who, as the highest ranked cleric in England should've crowned Elizabeth, but declined the "honour". He lost his see in 1559. What would've happened to the Elizabethan Settlement if those seven (or nine) sees had not fallen vacant at exactly the same time (many remaining vacant until 1561). How much opposition would there be to Elizabeth TTL? And how would Elizabeth have dealt with the situation TTL? @BlueFlowwer @isabella @RedKing @HortenseMancini

items.model_answer:
The phrase “Seven Bishops’ Death in 1558” does not correspond to a well-known historical event. However, 1558 was a pivotal year in English history because it marked the death of Queen Mary I and the accession of Elizabeth I. If the question is asking what might have happened if a major cluster of episcopal deaths had not occurred in 1558—or, more broadly, if the episcopal leadership of the English Church had remained stable at that moment—the consequences would likely have centered on the English Reformation and Elizabeth’s religious settlement.

When Elizabeth I came to the throne in November 1558, the English episcopate was overwhelmingly Catholic, appointed under Mary I. Elizabeth’s Protestant Religious Settlement of 1559 depended in part on replacing resistant Catholic bishops with clergy willing to accept royal supremacy and moderate Protestant reforms. In reality, many Marian bishops refused to take the Oath of Supremacy and were deprived of their sees, allowing Elizabeth to appoint reform-minded successors.

If those bishops had not died or been removed—if, for example, they had remained in office and successfully resisted deprivation—the Elizabethan Religious Settlement would have faced far greater institutional resistance. Parliament might still have passed the Act of Supremacy and Act of Uniformity, but enforcing them would have been much harder without compliant bishops to ordain clergy, administer dioceses, and implement liturgical change. The Church of England might have evolved more slowly, perhaps retaining more Catholic forms or facing deeper internal conflict.

Alternatively, if a hypothetical event involving seven prominent bishops had strengthened Catholic leadership in 1558, it could have bolstered resistance to Elizabeth’s reforms and possibly encouraged foreign Catholic powers, such as Spain or the Papacy, to intervene more aggressively in English affairs. This might have intensified religious polarization earlier than occurred historically.

In short, without a disruption in episcopal leadership around 1558, Elizabeth’s religious settlement would likely have been more difficult to impose, potentially resulting in a more contested, unstable, or even more overtly Catholic-leaning English Church in the early years of her reign.

edus.text: The phrase “Seven Bishops’ Death in 1558” does not correspond to a well-known historical event.
However, 1558 was a pivotal year in English history
because it marked the death of Queen Mary I and the accession of Elizabeth I.
If the question is asking what might have happened if a major cluster of episcopal deaths had not occurred in 1558
—or, more broadly, if the episcopal leadership of the English Church had remained stable at that moment—
the consequences would likely have centered on the English Reformation and Elizabeth’s religious settlement.
When Elizabeth I came to the throne in November 1558, the English episcopate was overwhelmingly Catholic, appointed under Mary I.
Elizabeth’s Protestant Religious Settlement of 1559 depended in part on replacing resistant Catholic bishops with clergy willing to accept royal supremacy and moderate Protestant reforms.
In reality, many Marian bishops refused to take the Oath of Supremacy and were deprived of their sees,
allowing Elizabeth to appoint reform-minded successors.
If those bishops had not died or been removed
—if, for example, they had remained in office and successfully resisted deprivation—
the Elizabethan Religious Settlement would have faced far greater institutional resistance.
Parliament might still have passed the Act of Supremacy and Act of Uniformity,
but enforcing them would have been much harder without compliant bishops to ordain clergy, administer dioceses, and implement liturgical change.
The Church of England might have evolved more slowly,
perhaps retaining more Catholic forms or facing deeper internal conflict.
Alternatively, if a hypothetical event involving seven prominent bishops had strengthened Catholic leadership in 1558,
it could have bolstered resistance to Elizabeth’s reforms
and possibly encouraged foreign Catholic powers, such as Spain or the Papacy, to intervene more aggressively in English affairs.
This might have intensified religious polarization earlier than occurred historically.
In short, without a disruption in episcopal leadership around 1558, Elizabeth’s religious settlement would likely have been more difficult to impose,
potentially resulting in a more contested, unstable, or even more overtly Catholic-leaning English Church in the early years of her reign.
