nodes.text: If John F. Kennedy had died on July 2, 1943, when PT‑109 was cut in half by the Japanese destroyer Amagiri,
the immediate impact would have been limited to his family, crew, and wartime morale—
but the long-term political consequences for the United States would likely have been substantial.
In 1943 Kennedy was a 26‑year‑old naval officer from a prominent but not yet politically dominant family.
His older brother, Joseph P. Kennedy Jr., was widely viewed as the family’s political hope.
If JFK had died in 1943, he would have been remembered as a war hero, perhaps posthumously decorated,
and his father, Joseph P. Kennedy Sr., might have publicized his sacrifice.
However, Joseph Jr. was still alive at that time
and remained the intended political heir until his own death in 1944.
If both brothers had died (as would have happened historically with Joe Jr.’s 1944 death),
the Kennedy political dynasty might never have risen to national prominence.
Without JFK:
There would likely have been no President Kennedy in 1961.
The 1960 election would probably have been won by Richard Nixon,
since Kennedy’s narrow victory depended on his personal appeal, Catholic outreach, strong debate performance, and machine support in key states.
A Nixon presidency beginning in 1961 would have altered Cold War dynamics at a critical moment.
The Bay of Pigs invasion might still have occurred under Nixon,
but its handling could have differed.
More significantly, the Cuban Missile Crisis might not have unfolded in the same way.
Kennedy’s cautious yet firm management—especially his resistance to immediate air strikes and invasion—was central to the peaceful resolution.
A different president might have escalated more aggressively
or, alternatively, avoided the specific chain of events that led to the crisis.
The risk of nuclear confrontation in 1962 could have been either higher or differently timed.
Domestically, civil rights progress might have taken a different trajectory.
Kennedy’s administration was initially cautious but increasingly supportive of civil rights legislation by 1963.
Lyndon B. Johnson’s presidency—and the Civil Rights Act of 1964—were enabled by Kennedy’s assassination and the political momentum that followed.
If Nixon had been president instead, civil rights legislation may have advanced more slowly, or in a different form, depending on congressional dynamics.
The space race might also have unfolded differently.
Kennedy’s 1961 commitment to landing a man on the Moon before the decade’s end was pivotal.
Another president might not have framed the Apollo program as a national imperative at that scale or speed.
Culturally, the symbolism of “Camelot,” the generational shift to youthful leadership, and the enduring legacy of Kennedy’s assassination in 1963 would never have existed.
The political careers of Robert F. Kennedy and Ted Kennedy would likely have been reshaped or diminished without JFK’s presidency as a catalyst.
In short, JFK’s death in 1943 would not have immediately altered World War II,

but it likely would have changed the outcome of the 1960 election, reshaped early 1960s Cold War crises, altered the pace of civil rights and space policy, and prevented one of the most defining presidencies—and assassinations—of 20th‑century America.

items.question: What If the IBM PC had never been released in 1981?
human_answers: The core problem with these discussions is that you wind up with a lot of people who had personal experience with home computers imagining their home computer was a long-term viable platform particularly killed by the IBM PC. The inherent market dynamic was, instead, that all the home computers were doomed to extinction at the hands of the standard business personal computer platform. It is businesses that care about backward compatibility with their internal installed base, while the home computer user market has an observable willingness to abandon old platforms and adopt new ones. This means home-targeted versions of the business platform can easily be adopted by the home market, while business-targeted versions of home platforms can only get adopted by businesses if they have a specific compelling business advantage. And then, as soon as the business platform clones the advantage, the home platform is again on the defensive. Home platforms are thus in an inherently weak position, and will be smashed flat by the standard business platform. And, well, there was already a standard business personal computer platform in 1980-1981 -- the 8080-compatible running CP/M-80. You could buy that platform as an Osborne 1, or as a Xerox 820, or from any of dozens of other of other makers. You even had the Microsoft Softcard (originally, "Z-80 Softcard", but Zilog complained) which used an Apple II as a host for a 8080-compatible running CP/M-80. The major problem that the CP/M-80 platform had going forward was that it had run up against the 64k RAM addressing limit of the 8080/8085/Z80, at a time when RAM prices had dropped enough that it was entirely practical to buy more. And since none of the chipmakers had had the sense to make a 8080-compatible processor with wider addressing, the only real way forward was the 8086/8088, since 8080 assembly code could be easily machine-translated into 8086 code. Everybody was just waiting on Digital Research to get CP/M-86 out. The IBM PC then arrived, with an OS that was arguably even more compatible in its system calls with CP/M-80, and the ability to use all the RAM anybody could practically afford. (Even if Gates never said 640K was enough for anybody, in 1981 that was true. Indeed, the first version of the PC's BIOS had a 544K limit.) It was the perfectly natural successor to the 8080-compatible running CP/M-80. The IBM endorsement made the transition smoother, and did have some secondary consequences (killing the S-100 bus, for example), but the true key to the IBM PC's success is that it was the natural successor-host for a software ecosystem that had grown up on top of the Altair 8800. What happens in the absence of the IBM PC is simple enough. Digital Research will release CP/M-86. At which point the CP/M-86 systems take over the business market, and eventually all the home computer platforms are killed by the multi-manufacturer business standard, just as in the original timeline.

As I understand it, the IBM machine was intended as an 'intelligent terminal' for their mainframes .. Businesses already had mainframes & dumb terminals but because the terminals were dumb the mainframe had to do everything - which led to limits on the numbers - and whilst IBM would be happy to sell (rent) you another mainframe they then run into the problem of getting the mainframes to talk 'seamlessly' to each other ... so IBM work on evermore powerful / more expensive mainframes as the number of users go up .. If, however, you can off-load some of the 'housekeeping' (things like deciding how to repaint the screen as the user edits a file, without the entire screen contents having to be resent from the mainframe, for example) onto the terminal, you can roll out cheap low end mainframes (at the same cost as the high end ones, naturally) able to cope with 100's more users .. Other companies wanted to 'get in on' IBM's business but had difficulties building mainframes as powerful as the IBM ones = thus, sooner or later, some-one else is going to come up with the concept of 'intelligent terminals' .. after which the PC becomes more or less inevitable ..
items.original_question: What if no IBM PC (2026 ed.) In short - the IBM PC (model 5150) was not an inevitable thing, the IBM leadership was highly skeptical of the project and it would not have seen the light of the day had things gone just slightly differently. So, what if that computer had never been created? My take - the personal computer market would look a lot like mobile or console market - a walled garden of 2-3 incompatible standards, probably Apple and Commodore (which, would do better financially without the competition from PC clones). It's interesting what would happen in Japan and (later) China.

items.model_answer:
If the IBM PC had never been released in 1981, personal computing would still have developed—but likely more slowly, more fragmented, and under different corporate leadership.

In 1981, the personal computer market already existed. Companies like Apple, Commodore, Atari, and Tandy were selling machines aimed at hobbyists, educators, and small businesses. However, the IBM PC did something distinctive: it legitimized personal computing for mainstream business. IBM’s reputation reassured corporate buyers who had previously relied on mainframes and minicomputers. Without IBM’s entry, large firms might have delayed adopting desktop computers, relying longer on centralized systems and terminals. The shift toward decentralized office computing could have been slower.

Equally important was the IBM PC’s open architecture. IBM used off‑the‑shelf components and published technical specifications, which allowed other companies to create “IBM-compatible” clones. This fostered intense competition, drove prices down, and standardized hardware around what became the Wintel (Windows + Intel) ecosystem. Without the IBM PC as a de facto standard, the market likely would have remained fragmented among incompatible systems—Apple, Commodore, and others—each with proprietary designs. Software development would have been more costly and divided across platforms, potentially slowing the rise of a unified software industry.

Microsoft’s trajectory would also have been very different. MS-DOS, licensed to IBM and then to clone makers, became the foundation of Microsoft’s dominance. Without the IBM PC standard, Microsoft might have remained primarily a programming language company or played a smaller role in operating systems. Apple, by contrast, might have gained a larger share of the business market, especially if it had adapted more quickly to corporate needs. Alternatively, another firm—perhaps a Japanese electronics company or a different American manufacturer—could have emerged as the standard-setter.

The absence of a dominant IBM-compatible platform might also have altered the development of the internet era. A more diverse hardware ecosystem could have encouraged earlier emphasis on cross-platform software and open standards, but it might also have slowed mass adoption due to incompatibility and higher costs. The rapid spread of affordable clone PCs in the late 1980s and 1990s helped expand computer ownership globally; without that price competition, household computing might have remained more limited for longer.

In short, personal computing would almost certainly still have expanded, driven by technological momentum and consumer demand. But without the IBM PC, the industry would likely have been less standardized, corporate adoption slower, Microsoft less dominant, and the structure of the modern technology sector significantly different.

edus.text: If the IBM PC had never been released in 1981, personal computing would still have developed—but likely more slowly, more fragmented, and under different corporate leadership.
In 1981, the personal computer market already existed.
Companies like Apple, Commodore, Atari, and Tandy were selling machines aimed at hobbyists, educators, and small businesses.
However, the IBM PC did something distinctive: it legitimized personal computing for mainstream business.
IBM’s reputation reassured corporate buyers who had previously relied on mainframes and minicomputers.
Without IBM’s entry, large firms might have delayed adopting desktop computers, relying longer on centralized systems and terminals.
The shift toward decentralized office computing could have been slower.
Equally important was the IBM PC’s open architecture.
IBM used off‑the‑shelf components and published technical specifications.
This allowed other companies to create “IBM-compatible” clones.
This fostered intense competition, drove prices down, and standardized hardware around what became the Wintel ecosystem.
Without the IBM PC as a de facto standard, the market likely would have remained fragmented among incompatible systems.
Each system would have had proprietary designs.
Software development would have been more costly and divided across platforms.
This could have slowed the rise of a unified software industry.
Microsoft’s trajectory would also have been very different.
MS-DOS, licensed to IBM and then to clone makers, became the foundation of Microsoft’s dominance.
Without the IBM PC standard, Microsoft might have remained primarily a programming language company or played a smaller role in operating systems.
Apple, by contrast, might have gained a larger share of the business market.
Alternatively, another firm could have emerged as the standard-setter.
The absence of a dominant IBM-compatible platform might also have altered the development of the internet era.
A more diverse hardware ecosystem could have encouraged earlier emphasis on cross-platform software and open standards.
It might also have slowed mass adoption due to incompatibility and higher costs.
The rapid spread of affordable clone PCs helped expand computer ownership globally.
Without that price competition, household computing might have remained more limited for longer.
In short, personal computing would almost certainly still have expanded.
It would have been driven by technological momentum and consumer demand.

But without the IBM PC, the industry would likely have been less standardized, corporate adoption slower, Microsoft less dominant, and the structure of the modern technology sector significantly different.

items.question: What If No P51 Bomber Escort?
human_answers: The P-51B/C/D was clearly a better dogfighter at medium and low altitude, but at 25-30,000ft the R-2800 engine in the P-47 maintained power even better than the Packard Merlin and the DB-605 engine in the Bf-109G. The P-47 was made to rule at 30,000ft. The P-47 shootdown almost the same number of fighters as the P-51, and the highest scoring USAAF groups in the ETO were P-47 units. Yes, the P-51 was shooting down more German fighters from mid-1944 on but that was because the P-51 was given the high-altitude job where they would encounter more enemy fighters while the P-47 was given most of the low altitude work like CAS, and interdiction missions. This is not to take away any credit from the P-51 but in most histories the Mustang gets the glory, and the Thunderbolt is relegated to being a ground support aircraft. The Mustang was clearly given the right name. She was fast and graceful and could dance with the best of them. The Thunderbolt had the right name as well. She was a warhorse that could absorb more punishment and bring her pilot home while raining thunder on the enemy. The P-38 Lightning is another also run for more complicated reasons, but she has her admirers for many reasons. And in 4th place the P-40 Warhawk held the line from 1940-43. Strangely it's the Mustang and the Flying Tigers Warhawk that are remembered best.

Hence my post about Big Week, P-47 provided 80% of the escort fighters during that effort. I doubt very many people realize that. P-38 is an interesting plane, read an interview with a high scoring German ace who said that provided it was being flown by a pilot who knew how to handle it he thought the P-38 was the toughest Allied fighter he faced. It also presented the Japanese with a difficult tactical problem in that it flew higher and faster than both the Zero and the Oscar. General Kenney liked it best because of the two engines. His pilots flew a lot of missions over water and he appreciated what two engines provided in that sense. General Chennault did not like for the same reason. He was at the ass end of a long logistics chain in a lower priority theater. To him two engines just meant twice the engine maintenance. The P-40 deserves much more credit that it gets. Only the P-51 and P-47 were produced in greater numbers (for US fighters), it was used extensively in the MTO, PTO, and CBI theaters well into 1944 and it was used by more Allied air forces than any other fighter. It was not a thoroughbred by it was definitely a work horse and sometimes that is what you need.

Cost to buy and operate the P-47 was not a factor - USA have had the money, material and fuel. They were after all buying and using the P-38, that offered no savings in any category. P-47 was made in more than 15000 copies. The P-47 was turned into a ground attack aircraft after the fact, and fact being that Merlin Mustang was rangier, a bit faster and a better climber. A combination of the P-51 getting the drop tanks earlier, and the better mileage on internal fuel made it the premier LR fighter of the war. Two very common 75 gal drop tanks make the P-51 going much further than if two 75 gal drop tanks are carried by the P-47 or the P-38. Some mix-up happened there. As-is, it could not do the job. With a bit of foresight, it might've come close. People at USAAF will need to request that P-47 is outfitted with wing racks from day one (ie. already in 1942, so it is debugged and ready for 1943), and there should be the drive to increase the internal fuel tankage. In OTL, the 1st increase was achieved by removing the stuff between the main tank and the top of fuselage so the main tank can get bigger, now with 270 instead of 205 US gals. That change upped the internal fuel tankage to 370 gals, that, together with 2x 150 gal drop tanks, enabled the theoretical 600 mile combat radius under the demanding ETO rules (that included cruising at more than 300 mph TAS at 25000 ft). There is also the need for the actual drop tanks to be available in the UK, with clear contracts with the suppliers. The know 'bubbletop' P-47Ds were the 1st with the main tank being at 270 gals. If there was the earlier go with adding some fuel tanks in the wings - even if it is not a 'surgery' as what was done with the P-47N, but perhaps 2x 50 gals? - together with a drop tank under the fuselage, the radius would've been increased even more, equaling the best P-51D values.

The P 47 was an incredible fighter and despite it's sheer size was fairly good in a dogfight. The P-51 Mustang was until the Rolls Royce Merlin was used a low level fighter at best. The V-1710 engine was fine but needed the two stage supercharger and the like which did happen it just took time. Drop Tanks and education on how to achieve maximum range needed to happen in order to make the Mustand what it became. The P-51 B was the start of the Merlin engines and gave it excellent high altitude performance. The P-47 on the other hand did not need an engine swap to be effective. Instead doctrine and production numbers made the difference. The most important use of the daylight bomber offensive, was the decimation of the Luftwaffe and this occurred in measurable ways. The P-38 was suffering from poor pilot training and tactics. THe presence of 3 high performance fighters whose abilities compliment each other is very desirable.
items.original_question: What if No P51 Bomber Escort? From Jan 1944 the Merlin engined P51 could escort the Bombers all the way to Berlin and beyond and destroyed the Luftwaffe in doing so. However, I would argue the P47 could have done the same job but The P47 did not get the escort gig because it was twice the cost and it was a superb ground attack aircraft. twice the cost in construction and fuel consumption. Really the game changer was the drop tank although the P51 was the best host for them by far I think of the P51 as the sleek technical European sports car sipping fuel, with the P47 as a brute, "cubes is everything", American muscle car guzzling gas like there was no tomorrow. The POD would be North American builds P40s instead of creating the new P51 design for the British. The distance the P-47 could cover evolved rapidly as new tanks were engineered: Early 1943 (No tanks): ~175 miles. (Could barely reach the Dutch border). Mid 1943 (75-gal belly tank): ~230 miles. (Reached Antwerp/Ruhr Valley). Late 1943 (108-gal belly tank): ~375 miles. (Reached Frankfurt). Early 1944 (Maximal 3-tank setup): 475–500+ miles. The P47 did not get the escort gig because it was twice the cost and it was a superb ground attack aircraft with its radial engine. OTL the Mustang was a dangerous aircraft to strafe German airfields while a much better dogfighter than the P47 [fixed after tomo mentioned]. I believe more P51s lost to ground fire than air combat. But I would argue that the Mustang was the best solution to the need for an escort, but the P47 could have done the job. Standardising on the P47 would simplify the training and operations of the fighter arm but at double the cost would it have been as effective and escort in numbers? I look forward to your thoughts.

items.model_answer:
If the P‑51 Mustang had not been available as a long‑range bomber escort, the Allied strategic bombing campaign over Europe would likely have been far less effective and far more costly, with significant consequences for the timing and shape of the war in Europe.

Before the P‑51’s arrival in late 1943, U.S. bombers such as the B‑17 and B‑24 attempted deep raids into Germany without continuous fighter escort. Earlier escorts like the P‑47 Thunderbolt and P‑38 Lightning lacked sufficient range to accompany bombers all the way to key targets such as Berlin. As a result, unescorted bombers suffered devastating losses to German fighters and anti‑aircraft defenses, as seen in missions like the Schweinfurt–Regensburg raids. Losses were so severe that the U.S. Army Air Forces temporarily curtailed deep penetration raids.

The P‑51, especially when fitted with drop tanks and powered by the Rolls‑Royce Merlin engine, could escort bombers all the way to and from deep German targets. Crucially, it did more than just fly alongside bombers: it aggressively sought out and destroyed German fighters, gradually achieving air superiority over the Reich. This attrition of the Luftwaffe’s fighter force, combined with attacks on aircraft factories and fuel supplies, crippled Germany’s ability to defend its airspace by 1944.

Without the P‑51, several major effects are likely. First, bomber losses would have remained unsustainably high, forcing the Allies either to scale back deep strategic bombing or to accept enormous casualties in men and aircraft. The U.S. might have shifted more heavily toward night bombing (as the British did) or focused on peripheral targets within limited escort range. Second, the Luftwaffe would likely have remained stronger for longer. A less degraded German fighter force in 1944 could have posed a much greater threat during the D‑Day landings and the subsequent campaign in Western Europe, potentially increasing Allied casualties and complicating the invasion.

Third, the destruction of Germany’s oil industry and transportation networks—key factors in crippling the Wehrmacht in 1944–45—might have been delayed or less complete. German forces on both the Eastern and Western Fronts depended heavily on fuel and rail mobility. If these systems had been more intact, Germany might have prolonged the war in Europe, possibly into 1946, though it is unlikely to have changed the ultimate outcome given the overwhelming industrial and manpower superiority of the Allies and the Soviet Union.

In short, without the P‑51 bomber escort, the Allied air campaign would have been bloodier, slower, and less decisive. The war in Europe probably would still have ended in Allied victory, but at greater cost and potentially after a longer and more difficult campaign.

edus.text: If the P‑51 Mustang had not been available as a long‑range bomber escort, the Allied strategic bombing campaign over Europe would likely have been far less effective and far more costly, with significant consequences for the timing and shape of the war in Europe.
Before the P‑51’s arrival in late 1943, U.S. bombers such as the B‑17 and B‑24 attempted deep raids into Germany without continuous fighter escort.
Earlier escorts like the P‑47 Thunderbolt and P‑38 Lightning lacked sufficient range to accompany bombers all the way to key targets such as Berlin.
As a result, unescorted bombers suffered devastating losses to German fighters and anti‑aircraft defenses, as seen in missions like the Schweinfurt–Regensburg raids.
Losses were so severe that the U.S. Army Air Forces temporarily curtailed deep penetration raids.
The P‑51, especially when fitted with drop tanks and powered by the Rolls‑Royce Merlin engine, could escort bombers all the way to and from deep German targets.
Crucially, it did more than just fly alongside bombers: it aggressively sought out and destroyed German fighters, gradually achieving air superiority over the Reich.
This attrition of the Luftwaffe’s fighter force, combined with attacks on aircraft factories and fuel supplies, crippled Germany’s ability to defend its airspace by 1944.
Without the P‑51, several major effects are likely.
First, bomber losses would have remained unsustainably high, forcing the Allies either to scale back deep strategic bombing or to accept enormous casualties in men and aircraft.
The U.S. might have shifted more heavily toward night bombing (as the British did) or focused on peripheral targets within limited escort range.
Second, the Luftwaffe would likely have remained stronger for longer.

A less degraded German fighter force in 1944 could have posed a much greater threat during the D‑Day landings and the subsequent campaign in Western Europe, potentially increasing Allied casualties and complicating the invasion.
Third, the destruction of Germany’s oil industry and transportation networks—key factors in crippling the Wehrmacht in 1944–45—might have been delayed or less complete.
German forces on both the Eastern and Western Fronts depended heavily on fuel and rail mobility.

If these systems had been more intact, Germany might have prolonged the war in Europe, possibly into 1946, though it is unlikely to have changed the ultimate outcome given the overwhelming industrial and manpower superiority of the Allies and the Soviet Union.
In short, without the P‑51 bomber escort, the Allied air campaign would have been bloodier, slower, and less decisive.
The war in Europe probably would still have ended in Allied victory, but at greater cost and potentially after a longer and more difficult campaign.

items.question: How would the population of the Falklands have been treated if Argentina had won in 1982?
human_answers: If GB got beat up per the OPs post and had to give up and go home I am not sure why Argentina would care about upsetting BG with the treatment of British Citizens on an “Argentine island”. They didn’t care about upsetting GB when the invaded and that was before the Royal Navy got beet like a stray dog and sent home with its tail between is legs. So why on earth would Argentina worry about what GB would think? I suspect a lot of folks will leave the Island and i expect Argentina would do everything it could to encourage that. Including being a bit heavy handed and sending over a good number of “settlers” and giving control of everything to its citizens and such. And I would not be surprised that Argentina was a bit brutal. Not the point of blatant executions as that would put them over the line internationally and they don’t really want that kind of reputation for no good reason, frankly I doubt the then current government really cares what happens to the locals or on the island its goal was to take it and use that propaganda to shore up the government. So yes it won’t be fun on the island and many will leave but I doubt it gets to bad, I suspect the local economy goes to hell but I don’t trully know enough about that to say.

What seems to have happened is that the Argentinian occupation forces initially expelled a small number of Kelpers, which attracted international criticism, then a further 14 potential 'troublemakers' were sent to Fox Bay East and placed under house arrest. Otherwise, the occupying forces seem to have been generally respectful - the principal exceptions being at Goose Green, where the civilian population was locked up in the social hall, and Patricio Dowling overstepping his authority as chief of police. The latter was apparently sufficiently objectionable that he was removed by the Argentinian forces. If the islands remained under Argentinian control, I would expect that those 14 might get deported, and favourable conditions offered for anyone wishing to leave voluntarily. Argentinian settlers seem like a given, at a bare minimum to replace departed Kelpers and possibly more - probably subsidised to do so, which won't help the condition of the Argentinian public purse. What, exactly, they would do there I don't know. I'd expect a boom in the popularity of mutton in Argentina as a 'patriotic' product of the 'liberated' islands. Over time the administration would surely revert to the mean of whatever was happening in mainland Argentina. It would be interesting to see what happens if/when Argentina undergoes its economic troubles. If the replacement of Kelpers with Argentinians hasn't progressed very far, I could easily see loud voices for ' erm... can we have the British back now?' on the islands.

I've studied this topic quite a bit and can say with confidence that Arg military did not go in with any concrete, long term plans on what to do with the locals. Their initial move was to try and keep a low profile (correctly) fearing that any incidents would only strengthen the UK's position, but this was more of on the spot decision by General Menendez than anything. My best guess is, if the UK fleet is defeated, eventually most of the locals will end up leaving on their own. Argentinean society is very Kafkean, and complex paperwork is needed for the most simple things. Unless islanders try to work with new local authorities, they will soon find themselves without the ability to drive cars (no driving licenses), lack of permits and licenses to practice trades, unable to open bank accounts, and unpaid property taxes piling up. Solving these things would entail applying for Argentinean ID cards, which could be interpreted as accepting Argentinean rule. I figure most people would refuse and just leave (unless the new authorities go out of their way to accommodate them.)

Probably nothing, except perhaps deporting a few troublemakers and using bureaucracy to force them to take Argentine ids. Even if Argentina wins the war, the Latin America debt crisis will be hitting by August '82, so I don't see that dictatorship lasting and, by that time, it wasn't as murderous as it was prior to 1980. The government, either the dictatorship or a new democratic government replacing it later, may enact tax breaks in the islands, like it had been done with Tierra del Fuego, to attempt to populate them. It doesn't need to be very successful, as they only had about 2000 inhabitants and Argentina had a population of about 30 million. As long as 3000 people move in, the locals become a minority. That may lead to ethnic tensions down the line, but they are just too few people in a too isolated place and facing a country that earned a reputation by going against one of the world's leading military powers and winning IITL.

Argentina would have gone as far as She could (and probably beyond) to accommodate them. It is of course possible that someone in the Islands would misbehave. That person would be crushed. The whole Argentina (Anaya) assumption was the Goa* Hypothesis. They are not going to come, there is not going to be a war, AND our US friends** shall help us. They were very, as in very, very, conscious of their international public reputation. Had they won the situation of the Kelpers and what the world was shown would be one of their primary preoccupations. As in fact it was during the war * https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annexation_of_Goa ** Argentina, and it's armed forces, was used by the Reagan Administration in the dirty wars in Centro America. Galtieri*** was absolutely convinced that he was an personal friend to most in the Pentagon. And most probably he was right. *** (He was not the one that was all out for Operation Rosario **** that was Anaya that made it an condition on the Navy supporting Galtieri when he, mini, couped Viola and take charge of the Junta) **** https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1982_invasion_of_the_Falkland_Islands
items.original_question: How would the population of the Falklands have been treated if Argentina had won in 1982? Let’s suppose that HMS Hermes and HMS Invincible had been sunk, forcing the British to make peace and accept the loss of the Falklands. Let’s also suppose that this victory gave the Argentine junta a reprieve of 2-3 additional years, but that it still eventually collapsed so that Argentina followed a political path similar as IOTL. What would the Falklands population have faced? It's almost certain that Buenos Aires would have sent thousands of Argentine settlers to Puerto Argentino/Port Stanley in order to, at least, make the Anglo population a numerical minority and to extinguish any secessionist aspirations. But would this Anglo population have been allowed to remain and then obtain full Argentine citizenship, perhaps even some degree of cultural autonomy, or would it have faced a complete ethnic cleansing in order to permanently erase the Anglo identity of the Falklands? There are fewer than 2,000 people, so if Argentina decided to do it, it wouldn’t have any problem doing so.

items.model_answer:
If Argentina had won the 1982 Falklands War, the treatment of the islands’ population—then about 1,800 people, overwhelmingly of British descent—would likely have depended on how firmly and quickly Argentina consolidated control, but most evidence suggests they would have faced strong pressure to accept Argentine sovereignty and identity, though probably not mass violence or expulsion.

Before and during the war, Argentina publicly stated that the islanders’ “interests” would be respected, but it did not recognize their right to self-determination as a separate people. The Argentine government viewed them as a transplanted British population living on Argentine territory. Official policy prior to the invasion suggested offering them Argentine citizenship, maintaining local institutions to some degree, and gradually integrating the islands politically and economically into Argentina. Spanish would likely have been made the primary official language, Argentine education curricula introduced, and closer administrative control imposed from Buenos Aires.

In the short term after a successful occupation, the islands would almost certainly have remained under military administration, at least initially, given that Argentina in 1982 was governed by a military junta. Civil liberties might have been limited, especially if there were signs of resistance. Some islanders who were openly hostile to Argentine rule might have emigrated to the UK, particularly if Britain had negotiated evacuation rights for those who wished to leave.

There is little evidence that Argentina planned mass deportations or ethnic cleansing. For diplomatic reasons—especially to avoid international condemnation—it would have been in Argentina’s interest to portray the takeover as orderly and humane. However, the population would probably have faced sustained political and cultural pressure to assimilate, including changes in schooling, administration, and possibly land and economic regulation favoring Argentine integration.

Over the longer term, outcomes would have depended heavily on Argentina’s domestic politics. If the military regime had fallen—as it did historically in 1983—an elected Argentine government might have adopted a softer approach, possibly allowing a degree of local autonomy while firmly maintaining sovereignty. Alternatively, if resistance persisted and relations remained tense, restrictions could have tightened.

In sum, the Falkland Islanders likely would not have faced large-scale violence or expulsion, but they almost certainly would have lost their political link to Britain, been required to live under Argentine sovereignty, and experienced gradual but significant political, cultural, and administrative integration into Argentina.

items.question: What If Meiji Japan still "Meiji's" but never expands, or fails to expand at China or Russia's expense, could it have grown to G7 rank?
human_answers: Let’s first think about the hypothetical scenarios that fit the “conditions” you mentioned. 1. Joseon modernizes before or at the same time as Japan. The relationship between Korea and Japan isn’t bad, but Japan is unable to colonize Korea because Korea becomes strong enough to resist. 2. Japan loses the First Sino-Japanese War or the Russo-Japanese War, and therefore fails to expand into Korea. For each of these conditions, Japan’s situation would be drastically different. In particular, if Japan were to lose a war, the "extent of its defeat" would make a huge difference. However, in my view, if Japan had developed in this way, there’s a high chance that the "Pacific War and other major conflicts" would never have occurred. There wouldn’t have been such "dramatic growth" as in real history—but there also wouldn’t have been such "catastrophic destruction" either. Ultimately, this is something that depends on the imagination of whoever envisions it. Honestly, I think it’s quite possible that Japan could still have developed to the level of a "modern G7 nation". Of course, it’s not inevitable.

East Asia would be completely different without Japanese expansion. Just to keep this in 1900 let's say they beat China but lose to Russia in 1905. I think that a Japan that doesnt even fight the 1894 war with China would be in too alien a modern world for a comparison with OTL to be very useful (mainly since no Chinese defeat in the 1894 war could lead to among other things a surviving Qing dynasty IMO). The Japanese public is highly demoralized by the loss against Russia, Korea remains an idependent country playing off Russian and Japanese influence, and Japan maintains an alliance with the UK and US. Japan not getting militarily or colonially involved in mainland Asia probably reduces the level of overall "momentum" that Japan is able to sustain as a growing world power. Many types of industries go hand in hand in their development and a Japan that does not pursue a world-class navy is probably also not going to be able to justify a world-class heavy industry to go with it. A weaker Japan is also taken less seriously and most importantly takes itself less seriously. I believe they would be somewhat simil啊r to Thailand or the modern day Philippines. Maybe they'd end up like OTL Taiwan and get really deep into some high tech sectors like semiconductors.

You are absolutely right, and it would be a natural effect to expect. Looking at your chart reminds of peculiarities of public opinion in the region in OTL however: Notice the contrast between China and Korea's Favorable-Unfavorable ratios and the opposing ratios of the South Asian and Southeast Asian countries, including 3 Southeast Asian countries Japan occupied in WWII? I have often heard people assert Japan is hated "throughout Asia" because of WWII, or is hated wherever its Army occupied anyplace during the war, but a closer inspection shows this is mainly a China and Korea thing. And for China, while with real historical basis, it's a generationally cultivated and amplified 21st century thing-- Polls were not so lopsidedly negative in the China of the 70s, 80s, and most of the 90s. There may even be some of that in South Korea also, with Japan a highly partisan issue amplified by the left-leaning party since the democratization of the late 80s, development of competitive partisan politics, and Kim Dae-Jung's breakthrough to political power, because the South Korean left's best revenge against supporters of former military dictators is to characterize them as part of continued lineage of 'collaborators' with Japan. By the way, as the author of Hatsunia, this book should be of high interest to you: "Ghosts in the Neighborhood: Why Japan is Haunted by its Past and Germany is Not"
items.original_question: If Meiji Japan still "Meiji's" but never expands, or fails to expand at China or Russia's expense, could it have grown to G7 rank? If Meiji Japan still "Meiji's" but never expands, or fails to expand at China or Russia's expense, could it have grown to G7 rank in the twentieth century? In other words, it takes all the modernization and technological upgrade steps it can to protect its sovereignty in the late 19th century world, but either is deterred or self-deters from annexing Chinese or Russian territory, or territory possibly in their sphere, like Korea, or if attempting to do so, because such attempts were rather fashionable among *many* (but not all) modern industrial states, they fail, would the same things constraining Japanese aggression or success *also* doom Japan's ability to increase its economic productive capacity and standard of living over most of the decades of the 20th century? Or not? Could Japan do as well, or better, in absolute GDP growth, per capital GDP growth, PPP measured GDP growth, and GDP global rank, by, for instance, 1920, 1940, or 1960 or 1980, without having any expansionary success beyond consolidating control over the Ryukyu Kingdom and diplomatically clarifying its ownership of the Kurile and Bonin Islands and never having won a territory in a foreign war? I think I can illustrate it best using this graphic. This helpfully long term chart of real GDP growth of Japan, Britain and the US shows Japan's growth curve in * red *. Would Japan's line be higher, lower, or about the same, without Japan's early successful wars with China and Russia, annexation of Korea, WWI absorption of Micronesia, 1930s exploitation of Manchuria and then occupied China, followed by the ultimately futile and highly destructive Pacific War, and the Cold War alliance arrangement the US and Japan set up to deal with the Soviet Union and avoid the recurrence of mutual war? Maybe the red line in the alternate history of an alternate Japan would have lower at some points and higher at others, but if so, please specify roughly when, and where do you think things would be stabilizing by the 1960 through present-day era. It may be tempting to call a Meiji (and beyond) Japan, with this type of foreign policy record that lacks success at military-naval territorial expansion as a Japan "pulling a Thailand" or analogous to a Thailand. But I would urge caution in making such an analogy. Sure, Thailand protected its sovereignty uniquely within its Southeast Asian neighborhood, while not being able to clash with colonial powers head on. But that's as far as the analogy would apply. Thailand's technological advancement and industrialization was for long, until the 1960s, pretty weak, and a Japan on Thailand's *economic* trajectory would be *categorically* poorer and less technologically, industrially, scientifically, and financially sophisticated than OTL's Japan. Thailand also only *began* experiments with constitutional government about fifty years later than Japan, even though Japan in the mid-20th century had some spectacular democratic and especially liberal failures and has some democratic deficits to this day. But their internal political cultures and societies are quite different.

criteria.name: Counterfactual Premise Fidelity
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses how consistently the answer adheres to the specific counterfactual: Meiji Japan modernizes but does not expand territorially at China or Russia’s expense.
criteria.1-2: Ignores or contradicts the premise; assumes expansion still occurs or shifts to other equivalent imperial conquests without justification.
criteria.3-4: Mentions non-expansion but inconsistently applies it; reintroduces expansionist benefits implicitly.
criteria.5-6: Generally respects the premise but leaves ambiguities about wars, colonies, or informal empire effects.
criteria.7-8: Consistently applies the non-expansion constraint and adjusts political, military, and economic trajectories accordingly.
criteria.9-10: Rigorously maintains the counterfactual across all downstream reasoning, explicitly addressing how absence of victories over China/Russia reshapes Japan’s trajectory.

criteria.name: Causal Mechanism Depth (Growth to G7-Level)
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates the clarity and plausibility of mechanisms linking non-expansion to long-term economic development or stagnation relative to G7 status.
criteria.1-2: Asserts outcomes (e.g., still G7 or not) with little or no causal explanation.
criteria.3-4: Provides simplistic or single-factor explanations (e.g., 'no colonies means weaker economy').
criteria.5-6: Identifies several relevant factors (industry, military spending, trade, institutions) but links are underdeveloped.
criteria.7-8: Explains multi-step mechanisms (e.g., military-industrial policy, capital accumulation, trade access, political stability) connecting non-expansion to growth outcomes.
criteria.9-10: Provides a nuanced, multi-sector causal model (state capacity, finance, technology diffusion, geopolitics, domestic politics) showing how Japan could or could not reach G7 rank under the altered path.

criteria.name: Long-Range Chain Coherence (1900–Late 20th Century)
criteria.criteria_description: Measures whether the answer constructs a logically consistent long-term trajectory from Meiji era decisions through mid- and late-20th-century global economic positioning.
criteria.1-2: Focuses narrowly on immediate war outcomes with no long-term projection.
criteria.3-4: Projects forward but skips major transitions (e.g., interwar period, WWII, postwar order).
criteria.5-6: Covers multiple historical phases but with gaps or weak transitions between them.
criteria.7-8: Provides a coherent timeline linking early 20th-century divergence to post-1945 global order and eventual G7-level status.
criteria.9-10: Offers a detailed, phase-by-phase alternative trajectory (pre-WWI, interwar, WWII or its absence, Cold War integration) with consistent logic across decades.

criteria.name: Geopolitical and Regional System Effects
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses how well the answer accounts for broader East Asian and global system changes resulting from Japan’s non-expansion and how these feed back into Japan’s development.
criteria.1-2: Treats Japan in isolation; ignores China, Korea, Russia, and Western powers.
criteria.3-4: Mentions regional actors but does not analyze systemic consequences.
criteria.5-6: Recognizes some regional shifts (e.g., Qing survival, Russian influence) but with limited feedback analysis.
criteria.7-8: Analyzes how altered regional balances (China, Korea, Russia, US/UK alliances) reshape Japan’s security, trade, and industrial policy.
criteria.9-10: Provides an integrated regional model showing reciprocal effects between East Asian power dynamics and Japan’s long-term economic ranking prospects.

criteria.name: Uncertainty Calibration and Contradiction Control
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer appropriately qualifies speculative claims and avoids internal contradictions while exploring multiple plausible paths.
criteria.1-2: Overconfident, deterministic, or internally contradictory.
criteria.3-4: Acknowledges uncertainty but still makes sweeping or inconsistent claims.
criteria.5-6: Moderately cautious; some tensions or unresolved inconsistencies remain.
criteria.7-8: Explicitly distinguishes plausible scenarios (e.g., loss vs. peaceful non-expansion) and maintains internal consistency.
criteria.9-10: Carefully weighs multiple branches, highlights key uncertainties, and maintains full internal coherence without overclaiming inevitability.

items.model_answer:
If Meiji Japan had modernized internally but never expanded at China’s or Russia’s expense—meaning no Taiwan, no Korea, no victory in the Sino‑Japanese or Russo‑Japanese Wars, and no formal empire—it still could have become a major industrial power, but reaching something equivalent to late‑20th‑century G7 rank would have been difficult and far from guaranteed.

Japan’s early industrialization after 1868 did not fundamentally depend on territorial expansion. The core drivers were domestic: land tax reform that funded the state, investment in railways and heavy industry, universal education, conscription (which fostered national integration and technical capacity), and deliberate technology transfer from the West. Even without colonies, Japan could have continued building textiles, shipbuilding, machinery, and eventually chemicals and electrical goods. Its later post‑1945 economic miracle shows that Japan was capable of becoming a top-tier economy without an empire.

However, empire did accelerate certain things. Taiwan and especially Korea provided food (notably rice), raw materials, strategic depth, and captive markets. Victories over China (1895) and Russia (1905) also brought indemnities, prestige, foreign investment confidence, and recognition as a great power. Those wins strengthened the military’s political influence but also integrated Japan into global power politics on advantageous terms. Without those victories, Japan might have faced tighter diplomatic constraints, less access to continental resources, and possibly more vulnerability to Western economic pressure.

The most serious constraint would have been structural: Japan was resource-poor. It lacked abundant coal relative to great continental powers, had virtually no oil, and limited iron ore. An outward-looking, trade-dependent growth strategy—similar to what Japan actually followed after 1945—would have been necessary. That path was viable, but in the late 19th and early 20th centuries global trade was less stable and more empire-centered than in the postwar liberal order. Without colonies, Japan might have been more economically exposed during shocks like World War I or the Great Depression.

The key variable is political. If Japan had avoided imperial expansion, it likely would have limited the rise of militarism that culminated in the 1930s and World War II. Avoiding catastrophic war and destruction might, paradoxically, have allowed steadier long-term growth. Instead of overextension, sanctions, and devastation, Japan could have evolved into a constitutional commercial state—more like a Germany without colonial ambitions or perhaps an early version of South Korea scaled up.

So could it have reached “G7 rank”? Yes, but probably later and more gradually. Without empire, Japan might not have achieved early 20th-century great-power military status, but it could still have become a major industrial economy by mid‑20th century through export-led growth. In fact, avoiding imperial overstretch might have prevented the destructive spiral that set Japan back in 1945. Its human capital, state capacity, and social cohesion were strong enough that, given access to global markets, it plausibly could have become one of the world’s largest economies—even without territorial expansion—though the path would have been slower and more commercially dependent rather than prestige- and empire-driven.

items.question: What If the attack on Pearl Harbor completely failed?
human_answers: Define failed - do you just mean the fighter planes are sitting armed in their revetments, the AA guns (both fleet and land based) are manned, the ships are at condition ZED, the radar stations are manned, and the Air Information Center has been set up (probably not fully manned but at least some minimal level of staffing). This gets you raid warning, fighters get into the air in time to meet the raid, and the ships in port and ready to take the punch. That is not done due any specific intelligence about an attack it is simply done as a response to the war warnings of late November. Between fighter defenses and AA fire and planes not making it back to the carriers the Japanese lose somewhere between 1/3 and 1/2 of their attacking aircraft. Damage to the Pacific Fleet is a lot less because the ships are buttoned up and a lot less planes are destroyed on the ground because they are either in the air or in protected revetments or at least dispersed. Losses to fighter pilots are higher because of more guys getting shot down but they also take their measure of the Japanese. That constitutes failure for the Japanese, particularly given the losses in trained air crews. What it means going forward I'm not sure but it sure is an ugly start. Or, do you mean by failure the US does all of the above but also has knowledge a Japanese carrier task force is going to attack Oahu during the morning of 7 December from a position between 200-250 miles north of Oahu. This means every available attack aircraft on Oahu is bombed up and ready to go (6 B-17s, 21 B-18s, 5 A-20s, 23 SBDs, 8 SB2Us) and Kimmel is able to position Enterprise and Lexington 150 miles to the southwest of where the KB is expected to be operating as well as sending the small number of submarines he has in port to the north as well. By the way, Kimmel also has a moment of profound insight and realizes the safest place for his fat slow battleships is sitting in port at Condition ZED. That scenario has the US forces on island ready to take the punch and the US has about 180 attack aircraft of various types ready to throw at the KB to include roughly the equivalent of seven squadrons of US Navy and US Marine Corps dive bombers the most effective weapon in the US arsenal. Scenario One is quite realistic and only needs some fairly minor PODs to make it work. Scenario Two is a lot less realistic but if you squint hard enough you can probably come up with some PODs that still make it work. Scenario One the attacking aircraft get butchered but the KB likely gets away clean. Scenario Two the attacking aircraft get butchered and Nagumo loses at least two carrier maybe as many as four depending on the breaks.

I do not disagree with the analysis above, but I would take a different path in logical application from the same starting point. Define failure. What if the Japanese failed to attack Pearl Harbor at all. What if on the morning of 7 December the seas were unexpectedly, and unseasonably rough enough to preclude any launch of aircraft. The invasion of Malaya started four hour earlier, and it is too late to cancel attacks on US possession in the western Pacific. Conditions are not much better on the eighth. Kido Butai trundles back home to Japan, undetected by US aircraft.. This may seem like a "what if Japan declared war, and did not attack Pearl Harbor" scenario but it is not. The key difference is, what if Japan launched surprise attacks all over Asia without declaring war, and its most powerful naval assets were non-combat effective for the first 25 days of the war? Comments?

I'm not too familiar either with how much intelligence the US had on Japan pre-Pearl Harbor, but I do know that a Japanese submarine was sunk by the US just hours before Pearl Harbor, and the message either was ignored or received too late to mobilize the dock. I could totally see an early warning, through this incident, cause Pearl Harbor to mobilize and allow for Japanese pilots to lose the element of surprise. Assuming the Japanese ships aren't found and only the planes are destroyed, this would make Japan more cautious against the US, since the Pacific Fleet wouldn't be as weak as it was after Pearl Harbor in our timeline. Additionally, because of the warning, there might be less civilian causalities and so, in the United States, there is anger at being attacked, there wouldn't be the rallying cry of "OMG THEY MURDERED A BUNCH ON INNOCENT AMERICANS!" But, overall, Pearl Harbor not being totally destroyed is definitely an interesting and plausible scenario that would have an impact on WWII.
items.original_question: What if the attack on Pearl Harbor completely failed? This was something that popped into my head. What if the USA has gained early warning of Pearl Harbor and had managed to defeat the attack? I am not too familiar with the intelligence background of it but I do believe I heard that there were some potential early signs before the attack that were ignored. If say the USA had received information a few days in advance and was able to crush the japanise attack and keep many of their best ships in a strong position in Hawaii now much would it change the pacific campaign? Would America be able to defeat Japan early maybe before the Nazis even fall?

items.model_answer:
If the attack on Pearl Harbor had completely failed—meaning Japanese forces were detected in advance, intercepted effectively, and inflicted little or no damage—the course of World War II would likely have shifted significantly, though not necessarily in Japan’s favor.

First, U.S. entry into the war would still have been highly probable. By late 1941, tensions between the United States and Japan were already extreme due to American embargoes on oil and strategic materials. A failed attack would still constitute an act of war. In fact, if the Japanese fleet had been damaged or repelled, American public outrage might have been even stronger, combining anger with confidence rather than shock and vulnerability.

Second, the U.S. Pacific Fleet would have remained largely intact. Historically, the destruction of battleships at Pearl Harbor temporarily weakened American naval power and forced the U.S. to rely heavily on aircraft carriers. If the fleet had survived undamaged, the United States could have responded more quickly and forcefully in the Pacific. Japan’s early-war strategy depended on crippling American naval capacity long enough to secure Southeast Asia and fortify a defensive perimeter. A failed attack would have undermined that entire plan.

Third, Japan’s broader military campaign might have collapsed sooner. Japanese forces simultaneously targeted the Philippines, Malaya, and the Dutch East Indies to secure oil supplies. If the U.S. Pacific Fleet had remained operational, it could have threatened Japanese invasion routes and supply lines. Japan, already operating with limited industrial capacity compared to the United States, could not afford a prolonged naval contest against an undamaged American fleet.

However, Germany’s role would also matter. Historically, Hitler declared war on the United States four days after Pearl Harbor. If the Japanese attack had failed but war between the U.S. and Japan still broke out, Germany might still have declared war under the Tripartite Pact, drawing the United States fully into the European theater. Alternatively, if Hitler hesitated, U.S. involvement in Europe could have been delayed or politically more complicated.

In the longer term, a failed Pearl Harbor attack likely would have shortened the Pacific War. The United States’ industrial superiority was decisive even after suffering heavy losses in 1941. With its fleet intact from the start, the U.S. could have moved onto the offensive earlier, possibly preventing Japan from consolidating control over key territories and resources. Japan might have faced defeat years earlier than 1945.

In short, a completely failed Pearl Harbor attack would not have saved Japan from war with the United States. Instead, it would likely have accelerated Japan’s defeat and strengthened American strategic advantages from the outset of the conflict.

items.question: The Highest Patriotism: What If George McGovern became President in 1968
human_answers: The one thing that keeps coming to me is Nixon would have the greatest meltdown in political history, screaming bloody murder then the Eastern Establishment has screw him for a third and final time. Even in OTL 68 a lot of the GOP had in fact become very weary over backing Nixon over his defeats in 1960, and 1962 in California. Now this last minute scandal, Nixon messing with the peace talks, cost him and the Republicans the election for a third time. At the very best, Tricky Dick might become a Secretary of State under a future Republican president and a Statesman, but the White House is forever gone. GOP swings back to the Rockefeller Republicans like George Romney and Nelson Rockefeller himself, but could also swing to Reagan. McGovern quickly makes a peace deal for Vietnam and pulls out. The South eventually falls. But we wash our hands of that conflict. McGovern would see to a second wind of the Great Society and likely see to a very liberal and Leftist Supreme Court along with many other Judges and at least some mild liberal reforms passed in Congress.

items.original_question: The Highest Patriotism: What if George McGovern became President in 1968 ​ The initial frontrunner for the Democratic nomination in 1968 was President Johnson of course, but an insurgent primary challenge from one Senator Eugene McCarthy set off a spark that would blow open a wide power vacuum in the Democratic party following Johnson's withdrawal from consideration. Johnson had endorsed Hubert Humphrey, his ambitious VP, but he chose not to run in the primaries, instead gaining support through backroom deals with delegates to win at the convention. This led to a bitter primary fight between McCarthy and Robert F. Kennedy, who had jumped into the race shortly before Johnson's withdrawal. As the primaries carried on, this fight would all come to a head with the hotly-contested California primary. Both campaigns put valiant efforts and loads of funding into this contest, but in the end, McCarthy would narrowly prevail, winning 45% to Kennedy's 42% and taking all of California's delegates. Kennedy would immediately announce his withdrawal from the nomination after the loss, but refused to make an endorsement. When it came to the convention, however, most of Kennedy's delegates coalesced around McCarthy, leading to a deadlocked convention between him and Humphrey. Kennedy had only privately backed McCarthy, even though he hated the man. With the convention at an impasse, Kennedy looked for an alternate who could emerge as a compromise candidate, despite his own ego making him hurt that no matter what, it wasn't going to be him. That man was none other than Senator from South Dakota George Stanley McGovern. McGovern was a Kennedy ally who had served as his brother's director for Food for Peace and an ambassador to the Peace Corps his brother founded. However, he was also firmly of the anti-war wing of the party and was more amenable to McCarthy and his delegates than Kennedy, whom McCarthy deeply despised. McCarthy vowed to stay in, but as more and more Kennedy-turned-McCarthy delegates flipped to McGovern, he saw the writing on the wall. After six more ballots, McCarthy would release his delegates, with all but a few holdouts voting for McGovern on the next ballot. However, the race was not over yet. There still was not an agreed upon consensus, and it would take more backroom dealing to put McGovern over the hump. To that, Kennedy looked to the Texas delegation, which was backing Humphrey, led by the old friend of his brother's, Governor John Connally. Kennedy aimed to make a deal with Connally to give his delegates over to McGovern in exchange for major concessions. Initially resistant, and more and more concessions being offered, Connally would finally accept the offer on one singular condition; he would be made VP. With the two coming to an agreement, Texas would announce the switch of its delegates to McGovern, putting him over the line to win the nomination after 10 ballots, and Connally was selected as McGovern's running mate. Republican nominee Richard Nixon had a strong lead in early polls, and it looked as if the McGovern/Connally ticket was heading for a demolishment. Some polls even had McGovern losing Texas despite Connally's presence on the ticket. But slowly McGovern chipped at Nixon. Nixon was seen as a crooked insider and someone who would do anything to win, while McGovern appeared to be more honest in his approach. However, the race still remained in Nixon's favor weeks before the election, despite McGovern's best efforts. Then, a bombshell emerged. Johnson, who had only tacitly supported McGovern, if only for his buddy Connally becoming VP if they won, had leaked to the press that Nixon attempted to sabotage the peace talks occurring in Vietnam. McGovern didn't wish to make the campaign dirty, but he still called the reports "troubling" and placed serious question into his opponent's integrity while not outright placing guilt, which helped his honest image even further, and painted an even greater contrast between the two men . In the end, it was close, but... McGovern/Connally (Democratic) - 279 electoral votes, 42.62% Nixon/Agnew (Republican) - 182 electoral votes, 41.04% Wallace/LeMay (American Independent) - 77 electoral votes, 16.01% ​ ...the last second scandal proved to be just enough for McGovern to win this election by the slimmest of margins. If he had lost any of the states of California, Illinois, Maryland, Pennsylvania, Texas, or Wisconsin, with Texas being decided by just 1.04% for him and only winning 39.74% of the vote there, this election would have been thrown to the House of Representatives, and all of them, decided by only a few points each, had flipped, than Nixon would have won an outright majority himself. George McGovern was never meant to win this election, but through a deadlocked convention, backroom deals, and scandals, it was the honest prairie man that triumphed over them all.

items.model_answer:
If George McGovern had become president in 1968, the United States would likely have experienced a dramatically accelerated withdrawal from Vietnam, a more expansive domestic reform agenda, and a sharper political realignment earlier than it ultimately did. His presidency would not have erased the deep divisions of the era, but it would have redirected them.

McGovern, even more than Hubert Humphrey, represented the antiwar wing of the Democratic Party. Had he won in 1968, he almost certainly would have moved quickly to end direct U.S. military involvement in Vietnam—likely faster and more unambiguously than Richard Nixon’s policy of “Vietnamization.” A rapid disengagement in 1969 or 1970 might have reduced American casualties and curtailed the bombing campaigns in Cambodia and Laos. However, it may also have accelerated the collapse of South Vietnam, potentially leading to political backlash at home from those who viewed the outcome as a defeat. The “who lost Vietnam?” debate might have erupted earlier and more intensely, shaping the politics of the early 1970s.

Domestically, McGovern would have pushed for expanded social welfare programs, civil rights enforcement, and anti-poverty initiatives. He was an early advocate of what later became ideas like a guaranteed minimum income. In 1968–1970, with a Democratic Congress still relatively strong, he might have succeeded in passing elements of a more robust Great Society expansion. Yet the economic headwinds of the 1970s—stagflation, oil shocks, and deindustrialization—would still have posed serious constraints. His liberal fiscal agenda could have faced growing resistance from moderate Democrats and Republicans concerned about inflation and deficits.

Politically, a McGovern victory in 1968 would have accelerated the partisan realignment that occurred under Nixon and Reagan. The “Southern Strategy” might still have emerged, but as a reaction to a visibly antiwar, socially liberal administration. Conservative voters—particularly white working-class and Southern voters—might have consolidated more quickly around the Republican Party. The cultural polarization associated with the 1970s could have begun earlier, and with sharper edges.

On the other hand, without Nixon in office, the Watergate scandal would not have unfolded in the same way. Public trust in government, which eroded dramatically after 1972–74, might have declined more gradually. There would have been no Nixonian expansion of executive secrecy or the same confrontation over presidential power—though conflicts over war powers and surveillance might still have arisen under different circumstances.

Internationally, détente with the Soviet Union and the opening to China might have proceeded more cautiously or differently. McGovern was less inclined toward realpolitik theatrics, but structural incentives for rapprochement with China were strong. It is plausible that normalization would have occurred later or through quieter diplomatic channels, though perhaps without the same symbolic impact as Nixon’s 1972 visit.

Ultimately, a McGovern presidency in 1968 would likely have meant an earlier end to the Vietnam War, a stronger push for progressive domestic reform, and an earlier crystallization of America’s modern ideological divide. It would not have prevented the economic and cultural turbulence of the 1970s, but it would have changed who was blamed for it—and therefore how the political landscape evolved in response.

edus.text: If George McGovern had become president in 1968, the United States would likely have experienced a dramatically accelerated withdrawal from Vietnam, a more expansive domestic reform agenda, and a sharper political realignment earlier than it ultimately did.
His presidency would not have erased the deep divisions of the era,
but it would have redirected them.
McGovern, even more than Hubert Humphrey, represented the antiwar wing of the Democratic Party.

Had he won in 1968, he almost certainly would have moved quickly to end direct U.S. military involvement in Vietnam—likely faster and more unambiguously than Richard Nixon’s policy of “Vietnamization.”
A rapid disengagement in 1969 or 1970 might have reduced American casualties and curtailed the bombing campaigns in Cambodia and Laos.
However, it may also have accelerated the collapse of South Vietnam,
potentially leading to political backlash at home from those who viewed the outcome as a defeat.
The “who lost Vietnam?” debate might have erupted earlier and more intensely,
shaping the politics of the early 1970s.
Domestically, McGovern would have pushed for expanded social welfare programs, civil rights enforcement, and anti-poverty initiatives.
He was an early advocate of what later became ideas like a guaranteed minimum income.
In 1968–1970, with a Democratic Congress still relatively strong, he might have succeeded in passing elements of a more robust Great Society expansion.
Yet the economic headwinds of the 1970s—stagflation, oil shocks, and deindustrialization—would still have posed serious constraints.
His liberal fiscal agenda could have faced growing resistance from moderate Democrats and Republicans concerned about inflation and deficits.
Politically, a McGovern victory in 1968 would have accelerated the partisan realignment that occurred under Nixon and Reagan.
The “Southern Strategy” might still have emerged,
but as a reaction to a visibly antiwar, socially liberal administration.
Conservative voters—particularly white working-class and Southern voters—might have consolidated more quickly around the Republican Party.
The cultural polarization associated with the 1970s could have begun earlier, and with sharper edges.
On the other hand, without Nixon in office, the Watergate scandal would not have unfolded in the same way.
Public trust in government, which eroded dramatically after 1972–74, might have declined more gradually.
There would have been no Nixonian expansion of executive secrecy or the same confrontation over presidential power—
though conflicts over war powers and surveillance might still have arisen under different circumstances.
Internationally, détente with the Soviet Union and the opening to China might have proceeded more cautiously or differently.
McGovern was less inclined toward realpolitik theatrics,
but structural incentives for rapprochement with China were strong.
It is plausible that normalization would have occurred later or through quieter diplomatic channels,
though perhaps without the same symbolic impact as Nixon’s 1972 visit.

Ultimately, a McGovern presidency in 1968 would likely have meant an earlier end to the Vietnam War, a stronger push for progressive domestic reform, and an earlier crystallization of America’s modern ideological divide.
It would not have prevented the economic and cultural turbulence of the 1970s,
but it would have changed who was blamed for it—
and therefore how the political landscape evolved in response.

human_answers: Here's who I think he would appoint to the Supreme Court: 1969: Arthur Goldberg replaces Warren (LBJ considered him in 1968 and Goldberg wanted to return to the court; a shoe-in for the Chief Justice spot imo) 1969: Archibald Cox to replace Fortas (Fortas may still resign despite the lack of DOJ pressure and Cox was Solicitor General under JFK and LBJ) 1970: Gerald Heaney to replace Douglas (Douglas retires early just as he wanted to IRL and Heaney was an advisor to Humphrey and other Minnesota Democratic politicians) 1971: Frank Minis Johnson to replace Black (Johnson was Black's preferred successor IRL IIRC) 1971: Shirley Hufstedler to replace Harlan II (first woman on the Supreme Court 10 years early) The other Justices being Brennan, Stewart, White, and Marshall the Supreme Court shifts dramatically in favor of the liberals by the early '70s, for a 7-2 liberal majority with only Stewart and White as moderate swing Justices and no remaining conservative voice on the court. This would have major implications for a whole host of Supreme Court rulings of the '70s and '80s.

items.original_question: What if Humphrey wins in 1968 The POD is that Vice-President Hubert Humphrey calls for a bombing halt in Vietnam in September 1968, rather than in October. Although Lyndon Johnson is furious behind the scenes, Humphrey's policy shift allows him to catch up with Nixon in time to win the 1968 election by a narrow margin. What would Humphrey's presidency be like? For one, Humphrey would've ended the war earlier than Nixon did. Combat troops would probably leave Vietnam before the 1972 election. Humphrey wouldn't have appointed Arthur Burns head of the Federal Reserve, resulting in a better 1970s economy. Humphrey would've appointed Earl Warren's replacement as Chief Justice, shifting the Supreme Court in a more liberal direction. Humphrey wouldn't have invaded Cambodia, meaning the Kent State shootings don't happen. However, Humphrey probably wouldn't visit China. But most of Nixon's domestic initiatives like the EPA and Title IX still become law. Humphrey doesn't veto the Clean Water Act. With the war de-escalated and the economy in good shape, Humphrey would probably be favored to win in 1972. His opponent might be Ronald Reagan, who wasn't as sophisticated a politician in the 1970s as he would be in the 1980s. If Humphrey wins a second term, the Republicans probably make significant gains in the 1974 midterms, giving them momentum ahead of the 1976 election. Humphrey would probably be remembered as a good president who ended the Vietnam War and expanded consumer protections at home. If Reagan makes a comeback in 1976, Congress would have more moderate Republicans, making it more difficult for him to implement a conservative revolution as he did in the 1980s.

items.model_answer:
If Hubert Humphrey had won the 1968 presidential election, the immediate trajectory of U.S. politics and the Vietnam War would likely have shifted, but not as dramatically as some might expect.

Humphrey, as Lyndon Johnson’s vice president, was closely associated with the Johnson administration and its Vietnam policy. However, during the final weeks of the 1968 campaign, he began distancing himself from Johnson’s war strategy and signaling support for a bombing halt and negotiated settlement. As president, he likely would have pursued a gradual de‑escalation in Vietnam earlier and more consistently than Richard Nixon did. Nixon expanded the war into Cambodia and Laos and intensified bombing before negotiating withdrawal. Humphrey probably would not have widened the war in the same way, which could have reduced domestic unrest and possibly shortened U.S. involvement, though a rapid end was still unlikely given Cold War pressures and South Vietnam’s instability.

Domestically, a Humphrey presidency would probably have continued and expanded Great Society–style programs. He was a strong supporter of civil rights, anti-poverty efforts, labor rights, and social welfare.
